Has a decision been
arrived at by the department authorizing the shipment of goods from ports in eastern Canada via the Panama canal to ports in IMr. Hoey.]
western Canada, even though the vessel carrying such goods should call at an intervening port? When the minister answers that question I have another to put to him.
I suppose this is the same question that has been asked before, involving the appointment of a customs officer in New York.

No. Let me make myself clear before the minister answers; I do not want to be discourteous to him. There are three questions; I will put them all and the minister can, if he will, answer them at the same time. There is the question of shipping goods-I will specify, so as to make the point clear-say, steel from Sydney, Nova Scotia, to Vancouver, all-water route, by the same vessel; and suppose that vessel calls at an American port en route. Then, there is the question of shipping Canadian goods from Sydney to New York by water, with transfer from a coastal to an ocean-going vessel, thence through the Panama canal to Vancouver, but the goods always being the same. Then there is the third case, the shipping of Canadian goods from eastern Canada, say, from Hamilton, by rail to New York, loading them on a vessel and sending them on in that way to the Pacific coast. Will the minister say just what is the situation in regard to permitting the shipment of goods in these three different ways?

Number one; a British ship loads rails at Sydney and goes via the Panama canal to Vancouver. There is no breaking of bulk; the cargo remains the same. In that case there is no objection. That is the first question.
Even if call is made at other ports?

Even so-if the bulk is there; if the cargo remains in the ship and is not broken, there is no objection. Number two: shipment is made in a British bottom from Sydney to New York, with breaking of bulk and transfer to another ship. In that case, it would be necessary to have a Canadian customs officer to supervise the trans-shipment, to check the goods and send copies of the manifests to the officers of the department in Vancouver. Number three: shipment from Toronto, Hamilton, or Montreal by rail to New York and transfer there to a ship. Here the answer is the same as in the second case, because you break bulk, and that would have to be done under the supervision of a Canadian customs officer, who would also mark and initial the necessary papers. Now, about

Supply-Customs and Excise
the appointment of a customs officer at New York, here is a letter that was addressed to me on the 18th of May-and my hon. friends will see that everybody is not of the same mind so far as that goes. It says:
Minister of Customs,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Sir:
We understand that representations have been made on behalf of Canadian shippers and importers for the appointment of a customs officer at New York, in order to encourage exports to British Columbia via American ports. We have pleasure in advising you that we have arranged to load the steamer Margaret Coughlan from Montreal to Vancouver, via the Panama canal, about the middle of July, and are in communication with the Canadian Manufacturers Association, and a large number of firms in eastern and western Canada, and are quoting them competitive rates in order to secure traffic for an all-Canadian steamship route between the East and the West.
For your further information, we may state that the above steamer is loading a full cargo of lumber from British Columbia to Montreal, and is also- accepting shipments of canned salmon for this port.
That is, the port of Montreal, from which this letter is dated.
Under the above circumstances, we do not think that there is any justification for an appointment of the customs officers in New York, as if we can obtain any reasonable amount of support for a direct steamship service, we expect to make the line permanent. In any case, we do not think it to the interest of Canada to encourage shipments via American ports, in view of a direct service being opened up. We may say that we have been requested to make this communication to you by'the owners of the above steamers, and also our agents in British Columbia.
Yours very truly,
Thos. Harling & Son.
Where is that letter from?
It is from Thomas Harling & Son, Montreal. I do not know the gentlemen.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is a well known shipping concern.

We may well hesitate in this matter when we consider that, taking as a starting point Hamilton, Montreal, or Toronto, the most our Canadian railways would get on the rail haul when shipment is made via the Panama canal would be about 20 per cent of the charges involved. In the case of Toronto, the freight by rail to the seaboard would be about 17 or 18 per cent of the whole. No decision has yet been reached by the department; we are hearing the pros and cons in the matter. I understand it may take some time before there is a definite and permanent line established. It takes goodwill and the encouragement of all people concerned on this side of the border to keep these people going.

There was a statement made by Mr. M. A. Macdonald in a coast paper
only a day or two ago to the effect that he had been in Ottawa last week and that the federal government had definitely arranged to place this officer at New York for the purpose of the trans-shipment of goods. He announced this as the official representative of the government party in Vancouver. He had just spent, I remember, a very pleasant visit here of a week or two in consultation with the hon. minister, and I wanted to get from the minister exactly what had been done so that the public would know.

If Mr. Macdonald has made any such statement it was not a statement that came from me, nor was it based on anything I might have promised. I said in the House here, and I repeat now, that the matter is still under consideration. I think it was my hon. friend from Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner) who had a question on the order paper a few days ago inquiring as to the cost of maintaining an officer in New York, and I replied that we could not answer the question then because we were investigating the whole matter. No definite decision has been arrived at yet. I do not say there will not be an officer stationed at New York, but I do not affirm that there will be, either.

Before we leave this question, the trans-shipment of steel products from, say, Sydney to another vessel at New York for the purpose of transport through the Panama canal would not be affected by the letter which the minister has just read to the committee. That does not affect the rail haul at all. That is all-water haul from a Canadian port in the east to a Canadian port in the west. The only thing is that it is carried in coastal vessels from Sydney, Nova Scotia, to New York, and there trans-shipped to an ocean-going vessel for carriage through the Panama canal to Vancouver. Will the minister not give consideration to - that, and grant the privilege?

My hon. friend did not give the whole case. He says it would not affect the rail haul to the border. But it would affect it in this way. If a Canadian ship leaves Montreal and lands the goods in Vancouver, and a Canadian ship leaves Sydney and lands the goods in New York, all the Canadian bottom will get will be the transportation of the goods from Sydney to New York whereas if you encourage a Canadian line it will get the transport from Montreal to Vancouver, which makes quite a difference.

There is a line of steamships registered in Canada, the Dollar Steam-

Supply-Customs and Excise
ship Company, running from Singapore to New York via Vancouver. It runs a regular line of freighters from Singapore to Shanghai and Vancouver, touching at Mexico, passing through the Panama Canal and going on to New York. They do not run up to Sydney because they are large vessels of 10,000 tons, and they cannot get full cargoes but they do get cargoes to New York. They will pick up a part cargo at New York from Sydney and carry it on their return trip to Vancouver; so it is a British bottom that carries the goods all the way through.
My hon. friend must not lose sight of the fact that they break cargo, and every time the goods are trans-shipped it must be under the supervision of an officer.
Certainly. That is what we want.
Whether it is a British or a foreign bottom, whether by water or by rail.
That is exactly what we want, and what I am trying to induce the minister to agree to. We want the appointment of an officer at New York for that purpose.

Can the minister inform us to-day what would be the probable cost of maintaining an officer at New York? I think it is desirable, unless the cost is prohibitive, that that should be done. I do not think the need is obviated by the fact that one steamship company is establishing a line between Montreal and Vancouver, though I am., very glad to hear of that, and I hope that another line will be started. I should like to know what the minister thinks would be the cost.

I have not formed any opinion yet. Our investigation has not gone far enough to enable us to give any data that would satisfy my hon. friend. I have not satisfied myself yet, and I do not like to give figures at random.
Is it a small amount or a very large amount?

My hon. friend must form his own opinion. He knows what it costs to live in New York, and that you cannot take a common labourer to fill a job of that sort. It requires a man who would command a certain salary, and there are the expenses, of moving down there, living expenses and so forth. My hon. friend is able to form an opinion just as well as I can.

This question has been discussed in the House on several occasions. It came up in the discussion on railway rates. My recollection is that the minister gave as his reason for not stationing a customs officer at New York that it would take away business from the railway companies, more particularly from our own railways. He also mentioned to-day the fact that there was not unanimity on this question, and quoted from a letter from Montreal. There may not be unanimity in Montreal on the question, but I can assure him that there is unanimity in the province of British Columbia, and unanimity on the part of Canadian manufacturers and of all people who are doing business with western ports. The fact is that to-day the business that is going via the Panama canal to the port of New York is business which under no circumstances would go across the continent on our railways. Our business men in British Columbia are to-day being forced to go to the American market to buy manufactured articles which they could buy in Montreal and Toronto just as cheaply as in the American market, but they cannot buy them in Montreal or Toronto owing to the freight rates on these articles being prohibitive. If they pay the freight rate over the railways, by the time these manufactured articles are landed in British Columbia the cost is so great that our people are much better off by buying the article in the United States or Great Britain, shipping it via the Panama canal and paying the duty. They get the articles much cheaper in that way than by buying from the Canadian manufacturer. I advocate the establishment of a customs officer at New York more particularly to enable us to do business with the eastern manufacturers in Canada to the exclusion of the manufacturers in the United States and Great Britain, and also to enable the British Columbia manufacturers, canners and so forth, to ship into eastern Canada markets by water the products which they cannot ship there to-day owing to the prohibitive freight rates on the railways.

I understand my hon.
friend to say that there was unanimity in British Columbia on this question of having an agent, a customs officer appointed at New York.

I might qualify that-unanimity with the exception possibly of a person such as my hon. friend cited who is interested in establishing a steamship line. I am in favour of the establishment of a steamship line myself and will do everything I can to

Supply-Customs and Excise
support it. In fact, I will go this far and suggest that if you cannot get a private enterprise to establish such a line you might use some of the ships of the government merchant marine for the purpose of establishing a direct service between Vancouver and Montreal in the summer and between Vancouver and Halifax in the winter time.
This question has been discussed for a long while and so far no action has been taken upon it. I must tell my hon. friend that I did not say we would not appoint an agent in New York-
I did not say that.

-any more than I affirmed that we would. The question is being considered. Now the difficulty under which we are labouring is this: The National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway come to you and say, "If you do this you will hurt us. The British Columbia people ask for special rates and at the same time they want to take freight away from us. The railway officials represent that whenever 100 loaded cars are shipped from Vancouver to the East it means that 60 empty cars have to be brought back from the East to the West.
Did I understand the minister to say-
That if you want 100 cars to be shipped loaded from the West to the East you have got to carry 60 cars empty from the East to the West.
I may inform the minister that same statement was made to me by a very high official of the Canadian Pacific Railway.
It was made to me by officials of the Canadian National Railway,

It is an official of the Canadian Pacific Railway that I am referring to. So I went to the Bureau of Statistics and found that the total going into British Columbia from the East and coming from British Columbia to the East is almost equal.
In what years?
Any year you like.
Oh, no, last year there was a difference caused by the shipments of grain.

I looked the matter up over a period of about three years and the statement is true that the tonnage coming from the prairie provinces eastward is very
much greater than the tonnage going westward. But that is not true of all British Columbia; the tonnage is almost equal going in both directions.

I would like to add my word of support to the remarks which the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) and the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) made on this matter. It seems to be an absurd policy to ignore the economic effect of the construction and operation of the Panama canal and yet that is virtually what we are doing so long as we keep away from the establishment of this customs office. So long as we have these iniquitous tariff duties let us make the tariff as ineffective as we possibly can so as to get our goods from one Canadian port to another without penalizing the man who sells goods or the one who purchases them.
I sincerely hope the minister will take this matter into favourable consideration and that before the year is out it will be possible for the canners of salmon in British Columbia to ship to Montreal or other ports on the Atlantic seaboard and correspondingly possible for the shippers on the Atlantic to ship to the Pacific seaboard via the Panama canal without any such consequences as are now complained of.

I just want to add one word and I think I can help the minister out of the dilemma he is in somewhat because there are regulations in the Customs Act which give the power to do this without any question. For example take subsection (q) of section 286 of the Customs Act.
I have got it here.

The section prescribes that:
The Governor in Council may, from time to time, and in the manner hereinafter provided, in addition to the other purposes and matters in this act mentioned, make regulations for or relating to the following purposes and matters:-	_ #
Subsection (q) Prescribing the rules and conditions under which goods imported in bond or duty-paid, and products or manufactures of Canada, may be transported from one port or place in Canada to another port or place therein, over any territory or waters outside the limits of Canada: Provided that the goods so transported shall, upon arrival in Canada from any place beyond the limits of Canada, be treated with regard to the liability to, or exemption from, duty, as if the transportation had taken place entirely within the limits of Canada;
Now, that is the old regulation.
That is the law.

That is the law, and the regulations have similar provisions as well.

Supply-Customs and Excise
Now, I just want to say two things in reply to the observations made by the minister. First, in reply to the suggestion that this demand was one of long standing and had never been acceded to in the past. I do not want to do more than refer to the fact that that is not argument, although it is used as such by the members of the cabinet.
No, I did not put it in argument. I simply mentioned it to show the difficulty we were working under.

Exactly, but I want to explain that it is said the previous government had done nothing and therefore we should not blame the present government. I do not want to blame the present government but I am asking that consideration be given to this fact: The reasons why nothing was done up to about two or three years ago were these. The Panama canal was closed in 1915 owing to a big land slide. During the following years from 1915 to 1920 the tonnage of the world was occupied on the Atlantic and. we had very little tonnage on the Pacific in connection with purely war purposes	so that there was	no	possibility, no physical possibility of giving effect to this during those years. Since the year 1920 down to the present time there has been a general release of tonnage all over the world so that there has been ample tonnage available, and it is during that period that this question has been pressed. That, I think, answers the contention as to inactivity in the past.
Now then one other point as regards railway tonnage. I want to say to the railways that they are not getting the tonnage. That is the point, they are not getting it to-day. We are forced to purchase very largely in the states of Washington and California many things that we would buy in eastern Ontario because the long freight haul by railway adds to the cost on the Pacific plus the duty. The lesult is that Canadians in the West are buying American goods because they get them cheaper. They pay the duty and get them cheaper because of the excessive freight haul; whereas if they could get the privilege of trans-shipping at New York we would buy the eastern manufactured goods, ship them via New York and, with the lower water haul charges, we would get them cheaper than we could import them from the United States. I want to impress upon the minister and these railways that if they would give this point consideration they would find out that what I say is perfectly true and accurate.

Then, as regards the haul by railway. There is an awful lot of goods hauled by railway from the eastern states and sold in western Canada-extreme western Canada, Alberta and British Columbia. That traffic goes over American roads; it does not travel over Canadian roads to-day. Some of it does but the great bulk of it is going over the American railways, so that if this privilege were established at New York it would not interfere, as I say, to any great extent with tonnage. What you would do is stimulate business in eastern Canada and business in western Canada, and anything that will stimulate business must ultimately benefit the transportation systems of the country.

I should like to ask the minister a couple of questions. First, I should like to know the particulars of the increase in the first item, and second, the necessity for that short and very elegant phrase "notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act"?

The increase in the first item is due to these causes. There are statutory increases which amount to $131,175, there is an increase due to reclassification which amounts to $18,215, some 114 additional officers have been appointed necessitating $96,130, and there has been an increase in contingencies caused by an augmentation in overtime pay amounting to $20,765. There are decreases due to promotions and appointments to vacancies at less salary amounting to $18,595, making a net increase $247,690.
As to the expression "notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act" the object of that is to enable our men to go on trains and boats on Sundays. Under the Civil Service Act we could not pay them for that work. They are paid by salary and we could not give them any extra remuneration for their overtime. When a train comes in from the United States at ten or eleven o'clock at night, our inspectors go aboard to examine *the passengers' baggage. That is the reason we have to do that, apart from the Civil Service Commission. I explained to my hon. friend that the wages paid on Sunday by the department are reimbursed by the various railways and steamship companies that use our service, but they do not appear against the expenditure, because they go to revenue. The expenditure seems greater than it really is. We pay money which we get back, but it is not credited to a special account, and thus a lesser expenditure is shown, because the moneys go to revenue generally. There is an increase in the number of officials in the various ports, Montreal, Toronto, Q.ue-

Supply-Customs and Excise
bee, and so on, on account of the increase in work, both in customs and excise. There have been various complaints, and I see by the papers that a lot of smuggling is going on. It is impossible to stop smuggling entirely but we determined that we would reduce it to a minimum. The same condition exists in regard to bootlegging and the various excise taxes that have been imposed lately.

I observe that part of this item is for temporary buildings and rentals. At the request of many of the business men of South Toronto and other parts of that city, I wish to call the attention of the minister to the very inadequate plant for a city of the size of Toronto. This year $50,000,000 net has been collected by the government in customs at the port of Toronto-more than seven times the total vote of $7,000,000 now before the committee. An agreement was made a few years ago, when the old customs house was tom down. At present we have not a customs house suitable for a city of over half a million people. Business is done in that customs house for a population of three quarters of a million, because the business done there includes business coming from the suburban districts, where there is a population of 200,000. We collected from that population of nearly three quarters of a million $50,000,000, in spite of the business being done in those old dilapidated buildings. They tore down the old customs house at the corner of Front and Yonge streets.
A lot was sold by the city of Toronto to the government at a cut rate to encourage the government to give the city the plant they required for the business. If yea go into those dilapidated customs buildings throughout the city you will find business men trying to do some business. The minister has a good staff there and they are doing good work. At the same time if new buildings were erected the increased volume of business would produce a revenue which would more than pay the fixed charges on the cost of the building. The city of Toronto sold a large lot on Front street to the government at a cut rate. They did not consider the commercial value of that lot because it was worth three or four times what the government paid for it. We gave them that lot because they guaranteed a proper building capable of accommodating the business in Toronto. It was promised that a suitable building would be erected on the land in one year. Six or seven years have gone by and nothing has been done. The city of Toronto does not seem to get anything anyway. With
them it is simply a case of "pay, pay, pay." One of my colleagues from Toronto said that the city got nothing, did not expect anything and would not get it if they did expect it. But you have to consider the business people of that district in the counties of York, Peel and Ontario. They are getting volumes of goods at that port of entry. Toronto stands as the great gateway of Canada. The local business is just $50,000,000 net. But other business is being done there, many villages and towns contribute to it, which would make dt more a matter of $70,000,000 than $50,000,000. I hope this tu'-penny-ha'penny, short-sighted policy of housing an important port like Toronto in a lot of small buildings which were used for other purposes and abandoned should be discontinued as far as Toronto is concerned.
We are in a similar position regarding post offices. From our post office at the Union station the receipts are nearly five and a half million dollars. I know that the present minister has been very active and has been trying to get increased facilities for the port of Toronto. He has been doing good work considering the poor plant he has to work with but the officials there cannot continue much longer. The condition of affairs for the wholesalers and retailers is intolerable. They are willing to pay for service. The erection of a new building is necessary, and the volume of business which is to be done there will be a paying proposition for the government, as it will pay the fixed charges on the cost of erection. I hope the minister will take this matter up and see if something cannot be done to meet the many protests made by the business men of Toronto. The present plant is utterly inefficient. We have not a plant there at all. The old plant was torn down and we have a number of rented buildings along the water front. The business men are willing to pay for it and we are not asking anything from the government. There will be more business for the government, it will be conducted in a better way and the public will be better satisfied. I think this condition of affairs is local to Toronto. Here we have a city of 600,000 population without any form of customs house except two or three little bits of rented buildings throughout the city. The minister has been very attentive and listens to any complaints the business men make as to the insufficiency of the plant. I hope he will give this matter his active sympathy before the next session of parliament. Could the minister tell me what arrangements are going to be made to tide over the temporary situation in

Supply-Customs and Excise
regard to rented buildings? Is it proposed during the next twelve months to give Toronto a proper customs house, instead of having the customs officials located in rented buildings?
I cannot give any assurance that anything will be done this year. I sympathize with the hon. member's views, and I admit that Toronto has not the facilities it ought to have to transact its business.
Nor Hamilton.

I have not been there, but I have been in Toronto three or four times. I understand they have a better customs house in Hamilton. I admit that it is very difficult for the officers to give 100 per cent efficiency in the quarters where they are located, especially in the long room, and in the examining warehouse. There is the other disadvantage of being compelled to lose time going from one place to the other. You have your express office on the water front and your customs in the railway station, and an office on Wellington street. I am not familiar with the location of all the offices. The examining office is near the Canadian Pacific Railway freight sheds. This is an impediment and a handicap, not only for the people of Toronto, but for the customs officers. They cannot work properly in those quarters, and I am as anxious as my hon. friend to see a proper customs house built in Toronto, but I have been asking myself many a time why the old customs house was torn down.
Hear, hear.

I have seen only part of
it where the express business is done, and it seems to me, from what is left of it, that it was a first class building, and why it should have been destroyed before the government were ready to put up another building I do not know. This year, however, there is nothing in the estimates. I am in sympathy with the proposition to build a customs house in Toronto. Toronto gave us $45,000,000 revenue. Montreal is in the same position as Toronto. Montreal has the long room in the examining warehouse, and has no proper place for the officers. They are handicapped. They cannot give us full efficiency, but we do not blame them, because they are working with artificial light and in badly ventilated quarters. But I took the premises as I found them, and until the country has enough money to build new premises or to improve on the ones we have now, I do not think I can give any encouragement, at least for this year, to my hon. friend.

I appreciate the line of
argument of the minister; but when during the last fiscal year approximately fifty million dollars was made by the department out of the city of Toronto, surely a portion of that sum should be given back to the people who are paying that money, the business men of Toronto, by giving them increased plant to take care of the increasing business. At the present time a large portion of that sum is being utilized in other parts of the country, and surely the city which does the business and is paying in this huge sum to the department, should receive back some share of it in increased facilities. I think about one-third or, perhaps, forty per cent of that fifty million dollars was pure profit, and I do not see how the business is going to be conducted unless increased facilities are afforded. It will take two or three years to build a new customs house, and by that time the receipts will have increased well on to seventy-five million dollars. I would invite the minister to visit Toronto-we are always glad to see him-in order to see if something cannot be done. I understand the minister is doing the best he can; but at the same time the business men are protesting; they are paying for this, and a large proportion of the fifty million dollars is profit and is being used to give increased facilities in other parts of the country.

The hon. member says that he is at a loss to know why the old customs house disappeared. I do not know why he is at a loss. A proper customs house was to have been built; arrangements were made for it; the work was under way; the property was cleared, when the war came on and we stopped expenditures. There is no mystery about the matter at all. Can my hon. friend state how much money he is paying in Toronto now for rents? I do not know whether the other property is rented or is owned by the government. If it is on governmental property, that has a value; it is something that could be made use of and revenue could be brought in from it. The chances are, however, that some rent is still going out. If the minister were to take the value of other properties, whether rented or not, which could be put to other uses, easily sold, for instance, at the present time; if he were to consider the cost those properties mean and on top of that consider the extra cost he admits this means in carrying on business in Toronto, I am sure he would realize that, as a matter of good business, this place should be built at once.

Supply-Customs and Excise
Sure.

Then that
question is beyond all debate.
Find the money.
My hon. friend talks about finding money. That port certainly is producing a great deal of money, and the money from that port is going to buy buildings elsewhere.
No.

Let us see.
Does my hon. friend not think it would be better to have a customs warehouse where he can properly carry on business, something that will help business and help the country, than to buy a corner of King and Yonge streets for over a million dollars, and then put on top of that a building costing two or three million dollars for railway purposes? Does my hon. friend not think it is a good deal better to apply the funds which are got out of customs earnings in the port of Toronto, to giving decent facilities there than, to buy a large hotel in Quebec-I mean France-to look after railway business there? These things are being done.

I am glad my hon.
friend is uniting both Quebec and France.

I corrected myself. You see my hon. friend's mere presence is enough to remind me of his beautiful province of Quebec and to make it an uppermost subject in my mind. Why should this customs warehouse not be constructed; why should not this expenditure be made when business absolutely requires it, when my hon. friend says that it ought to be done but that the trouble is money. Is this not a little more important than a palatial ticket office at the comer of King and Yonge streets? Is it not more important than having this building in Paris at the present time? What real railway business does the minister think we are going to get out of that building in Paris, which would compare in importance with a proper plant at Toronto for his department?

We had a Minister of Public Works for a few months representing this party, or rather Union government. He was Minister of Public Works for a few months on his way from the cool shades of opposition to the chairmanshij? of the Railway Commission. During the short period that he occupied that position he tore down the very excellent building which we had in Toronto,
a building not adequate to the necessities of the case, an old building, but nevertheless infinitely better than anything we have now or anything you can get in the shape of a warehouse. The minister is occupying now for customs purposes a warehouse on Wellington street, and an old baking powder factory for his examining warehouse.
Was that what it was?
Yes, Magic baking powder was made where the warehouse is to-day.
The magic has gone and the powder also.

I was through the warehouse a short time ago, and it is entirely inadequate for its purposes. If the government could see things from the right perspective, we would certainly have had a new customs house in Toronto before we started building a hotel in Paris for the National Railways. The latter may contribute some little amount to the revenues of the National Railways, but even that is doubtful. It is a veiy speculative enterprise; but the customs needs of Toronto are pressing upon the people there, and every month and every year that we are without these facilities, the increasing business will make that necessity still more pressing. Ordinary business prudence leads a manufacturer to add to his building if he has not sufficient space, wherein to carry on his business. It is always an expensive matter to conduct business in inadequate premises, and that is what the minister tells us is being done to-day.
That is so.

I have an idea that a very large part of the interest cost of a new customs warehouse is being spent now through the congestion that is inevitable under present circumstances. If this government had been considering the welfare of its own services, the Minister of Public Works would have brought down an item this year for a new customs house in Toronto. We could stand the post office for another year -or two, but certainly a new customs house for Toronto is one of the crying necessities of the business of this country. Moreover, we did a very large business last year and the customs receipts are very large; but with every year that passes, the customs receipts of Toronto will be greater, and if the customs business of Toronto expands in the present limited quarters that are now available, the cost of administering the department will be constantly increasing. I do not suppose it is of any

Supply-Customs and Excise
avail to say these things but I think the government is to be condemned for treating the city of Toronto and its customs necessities in the way that it has.

My hon. friend from West York (Sir Henry Drayton) asked how much we paid in rents in Toronto. I do not know; that is a matter that comes under the Department of Public Works. The hon. member (Mr. Hocken) says that it is a shame to treat Toronto in the way it has been treated. Let me tell him that I do not build custom houses; I simply ask that they be put up, and when there is no money forthcoming they are not built. The city of Toronto has produced this year S45,000,000 and the city of Montreal $78,000,000; but I would point out that the custom house in Montreal is in no better shape than that in Toronto, being indeed, if anything, rather worse, because they are using the examining warehouse as a long room.
That is another reason for condemning the government.

That is a question I am not discussing. But I want to assure my hon. friend that we are not aiming at Toronto, as he seems to think.
Mr. HOCKEN; I did not say that.
The hon. member said that it was shameful the way we treated Toronto.
I say it is a shameful way to treat any city.

I simply want to explain that what my hon. friend calls "shameful treatment" has been due entirely to lack of funds. However, I will not discuss the point further, because it is a question that will come up in connection with the Public Works estimates. I am with the hon. member in wishing to see to the comfort of the officials. I will stand by every official of the Department of Customs and Excise in an endeavour to see that he gives efficient service, and undoubtedly these people are handicapped when they have to work in quarters such as they have in Toronto and Montreal. We have no right to have a man work in artificial light from nine in the morning to five in the afternoon, or ask him to do his work in an unventilated place. I have protested against it, and when my hon. friend asks to have a custom house built in Toronto, or any other hon. member begs for a custom house in Montreal, I will stand by him.

The city of Toronto in 1914 sold to the government a lot for $110,000.

To-day that lot is worth well on to half a million. The government has had the benefit of the increment in those nine years. The lot was sold for $110,000, but it was worth more than that at the time it was sold to the government, and a member of the government of that day, the Hon. Mr. Reid, promised to have a building erected on it within twelve months. There is no building on the lot to-day, and I think that every effort should be made to put one up because it would increase the value of the property to the government.
I have not taken any pledge to carry out the promises of my predecessors, nor do I intend to.
Do the officers of the Excise department who go through the country looking for private stills come under this item?
Yes.

I do not want to have it understood for a moment that I am pleading for the bootleggers or those who operate private stills; I hope the minister will put them all in gaol, because they make rotten stuff.
There would be few left in certain places if I did that.

In my county, however, some of the officers came to a place called Vita and caught two men with stills. They brought them before Magistrate Willfong in Vita on New Year's Day for trial. The men asked for a postponement of the trial in order that they might obtain counsel. I believe that the officers requested the magistrate not to consider a postponement, but to go on with the trial, and this he did. He found the men guilty and sentenced them to nine and twelve months respectively, and they left their families in that district fairly destitute. I repeat, I am not pleading for the bootlegger, but I think the officers of the department should give every man a fair trial, and when he asks for a postponement in order to obtain counsel that request should be considered. I do not think, in any event, that it is right to try a man in this country on New Year's Day, because that is the day we celebrate.
I do not know what the facts are, and my hon. friend evidently is not quite conversant with them. Were the officers federal or provincial officers?

They were Inland
Revenue officers.

Supply-Customs and Excise

There is no longer an Inland Revenue department, but be that as it may, there are some provincial officers who are sworn in as preventive officers empowered to look for stills. I lived in Manitoba a few years, and so far as I know, New Year's was always a dies non; you could not try cases on that day. Now, you cannot put sense into a man's head if he is incapable of it; a man is bom with a certain amount of brains and you cannot add to his mental stature. But I should think that a magistrate would exercise common sense and postpone a trial if it appeared that injustice would be done by proceeding with it. I blame the magistrate more than I do the officers in this case, because he is a man of higher education who should not be carried away by too great zeal in
5 p.m. the execution of his duties. If what my hon. friend says has happened, I am sorry. But when things of this kind do occur they should be reported to the department ; otherwise people have no right to complain afterwards. I am prepared to stand by my officers when they properly execute their duties, and when they do not I am willing to reprimand, suspend or dismiss them as the necessity of the case might demand.
Has the minister had any representations with regard to the matter of the New York agent? Has he heard anything from Walkerville and the manufacturers at that point?
No.
The minister has had no complaints?
No.

Representations have come from points as far as Windsor that they are losing business because they cannot make use of the Panama canal. I do not know whether or not that is correct, but from what is stated it would seem to be. If these representations are true, and goods can be shipped from a point as far west as Windsor to New York and then trans-shipped by the Panama canal to Vancouver cheaper than they can be sent on the rail haul, then it strikes me that this is a matter that should be looked into by the minister. The business people represent that it is impossible to do business at present and that they are losing business. They say that it is absolutely necessary to have a customs officer appointed in New York. I sympathize a great deal with what my hon. friend says about the railway situation, but I doubt very much
Whether the railways are making anything at all in view of the statements I have heard from the railway officials themselves. Before the committee last year we had evidence of the railroaders as to the cost of hauling freight to Vancouver, and I doubt very much whether there is any money in the railway business to-day so far as that haul is concerned. It is claimed that the freight cost has been cut to the lowest possible point and that there is practically nothing in the business now. If that is true, and I see no reason to dispute what the railroaders themselves say, would it not be better for them to get a profitable haul even though it may be shorter? In other words, are not the railways losing money by trying, at the present high rate, to carry these commodities right over the continent in competition with the water rates? We all want to help the National Railways; there is no question about that; but I greatly doubt whether my hon. friend is helping them. It does seem to me that if the representations made before that committee are correct, there would be more money for the railways through this shorter haul.
My hon. friend proceeds on the assumption that I have refused the appointment of a customs officer in New York, but I have not done so.
The minister pointed out earlier in the session that the reason why it had not been done was because it would be a loss in respect to the long railway haul.
That was the representation made to me.
I would like him to look into it very carefully to see whether or not there is anything in that allegation.

I am doing that. There is something in what my hon. friend says, that if we double or treble the traffic to the frontier there will be that much more rail business done. But the representations that have been referred to have not come to me or to the department; there may have been something in the press about it, but there have been no official representations. All the information is being got together, and after we have made a thorough investigation and got all the necessary data, the matter will be submitted to council. I do not like to go ahead without being sure of my ground, but when all the information has been obtained a decision will be taken. I have no personal views on the matter, one way or the other; it is just

Supply-Customs and Excise
a question of what will be in the best interests of the country.

I think the minister will agree that the most important consideration involved is the maintenance of interprovincial trade. To pass to another part of this item, I notice there is provision for 114 new employees. Are they all appointed by the Civil Service Commission?
Every one of them.
So that no use is being made of the wording of this item except so far as it applies to overtime.
Only the overtime-unfortunately.
Very fortunately, for the service.

The minister said a little while ago that he was not obliged to carry out the promises of his predecessor, but I say that he should carry out those promises when he sees the necessity for doing so. There should be continuity in government business just as there should be in any other business.

I said I was not bound by
the pledges of my predecessors.

But the minister know's the necessity for it. I would ask him whether, if it were a matter of his own business, he would continue to do business the way the government are doing it. We are not getting sixty per cent of efficiency from his officers; in Toronto the citizens who are doing business with the customs house are getting a minimum of service at a maximum of cost. We are running from Yonge street clear out to the comer of John and King streets; nobody seems to know where to go to get any customs business done. There is a site available for the erection of a proper customs building, but it is lying idle while large sums are being paid out for rent. The present quarters of the customs officers in Toronto are unsanitary and unsatisfactory in every way. Is that good business? I say it is not. The government should do away with the rotten old buildings they are using in Toronto and get a serviceable, sanitary building where the citizens can carry on their business in a proper manner; but instead of that, money is being spent in the rental of quarters in which the public cannot get service. I say it is an absolute waste of money. I have been around that customs house for thirty-five years and I know the inconveniences that the people are subject to. It is a crime the way the people have to stand for hours

on the sidewalk trying to get into these old buildings in order to get their business done. You could now do without hundreds of the men now employed if you had a proper building.
I think my hon. friend did not understand me when I spoke a moment ago.
I understand you thoroughly, sir.

I said I was in favour of building a customs house. What more does the hon. member want me to do? I do not build the customs houses; I do not rent them or furnish them; I do not hang lamps in them. I am in sympathy with my hon. friend, and I do not see what he is getting excited about. I would like to see Toronto have a better customs house, because I would get better service from my officials.

That is what might be called passing the buck. We all realize that it is the Public Works department that puts up the buildings. That is what the Post Office Department says when a post office is asked for. Now, if the minister makes a real-demand on the Department of Public Works for a building, he may get something done. The minister is the man who should be the judge; he should know what he wants, and he should have sufficient prestige with his government to see that he gets it. If I were in his position I would see that I did get it, or I would not be there.

That suggestion might apply both ways. The friends of my hon. friend were in office not long since; there was a Minister of Public Works and he made a promise in the matter. The former building that was torn down may have been a little cramped, but it was a beautiful building, if I remember it rightly. Now, I am willing to have a new building, but we cannot build these things with wind. We have to have the money, and as soon as we get the money I am satisfied that the Minister of Public Works will be only too glad to get rid of my demands and petitions for customs houses

A contract should be a contract, even if it was made by the government. I realize that the putting up of these buildings is not done by the minister's department, but I am speaking of the government as a whole. Here is a contract made for the sale of lands in 1914, the parties to it being the city of Toronto on the one hand and the federal government on the other. The area involved

Supply-Agriculture-Dairying
was a large tract of land on the south side of Front street, the purchase price being 8110,000-away less than the commercial value of the land. The government were to put up a build ng there, and as I understand the contract it could be enforced in the Exchequer Court of Canada. But two bodies serving the public do not want to quarrel; they should work together to get a government building that will facilitate the public business. The city is interested in having a good government building there, and they are spending a lot of money in that district; they have put down a new pavement, they have given a new car service, and so on. I hope that during the recess something will be done in this matter, because twenty-six or twenty-seven public bodies have asked the Toronto representatives to urge upon the government the necessity for action. When the department is doing business to the extent of 850,000,000 a year, surely it should do something to save the time of the business men. Millions of dollars worth of time has been wasted every year through the inconvenience the public have suffered in trying to get service from the customs house in Toronto. I say that l hope the government will take the matter up in the recess and see whether something cannot be done.

I do not wish it to be understood that I am criticising the ability of the Minister of Customs, because I know that he is full of ability and "pep." I assure him that I am not a bit excited about it. I know the conditions around the customs house and the post office; I have spent my life there, and I have a right to speak of conditions as I find them. I believe in calling a spade a spade, and I do think that the government are deserving of criticism for their lack of interest in Toronto. It is a persecution of Toronto; that is what it is all the time.
Item agreed to.
Agriculture-dairying, $230,000.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. R. MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
I think the committee will remember that this item was allowed to stand over at the request of the hon. member for Glengarry (Mr. Kennedy). I am sorry the hon. gentleman is not in his seat, but I was discussing the matter with him yesterday and he said that on the budget or on some other occasion I had dealt pretty fully with the question that he was desirous of taking up. He suggested among other things that he would like to know if the report of Mr. Ruddick and Mr. Wilson who went to Australia and New Zealand to examine into the dairy industry there would be ready for the House this session. Before coming to that,. Mr. Chairman, I might deal with some of the activities that we intend to undertake this year partly as a result of the investigations of Mr. Ruddick and partly also as a result of the grading system that was provided for some years ago, but which only came into force on the 1st of April last. Under the Dairy Industry Act of 1921 provision was made for the grading of all cheese and butter for export. That has been let stand over from time to time so that the public would get familiarized with the idea of grading these dairy products. The system was accepted generally throughout the country, but naturally a new departure like this would meet with some opposition. This has gradually disappeared, more especially as the Ontario government was introducing at the same time the principle of purchasing milk for cheese factories on a basis of grade and a basis of butter fat. The two coming together helped each other, though to some extent where there was difficulty it seemed to accentuate the trouble. However, the du ficulty has been largely localized, and no r that grading has been in force for nearly two months the opposition has disappeared altogether. Just what results will come out of that so far as a more acceptable reception of our butter on the British market is concerned, time alone will tell. We have not had sufficient experience yet to indicate what the results will be, but I have no thought of anything else but that there will be a very decided improvement. The moment you can get quality paid for on a basis of quality there will be some encouragement to the farmers and cheesemakers to produce quality.
The intention is to extend the activities of the Dairy branch in several particulars, one of them as a result of Mr. Ruddick's interim report, and that is with respect to the pasteurizing of milk for the manufacture of cheese. Formerly in Canada pasteurization was confined largely if not entirely to cream for the manufacture of butter, and it was also practised with regard to the whey product in order to ensure against tuberculosis the animals that used whey from cheese factories. We have found, however, that one of the reasons why Australia and New Zealand have been able to surpass Canada in the manufacture of cheese has been the fact that they have also pasteurized the milk that has gone into the manufacture of cheese. There is no question that the pasteurization of cream makes butter very much better. It gives it better
Supply-Agriculture-Dairying

keeping qualities, and raises the quality generally. The Australians and New Zealanders have found out that pasteurization has the same effect when applied to milk in the manufacture of cheese. That is one of the things to which we attribute the general excellence of the cheese they have placed on the market, and why they have not only come up to Canadian cheese, but I fear surpassed it in quality. I do not use the word fear in any other sense except that we are not where we were, and it is our business to get back to where we were at the top of the list.
There is a combined cheese and butter factory at the town of Finch between thirty and forty miles south of here. It was erected some seven or eight years ago for demonstration purposes. It was felt by a good many that in order that dairying should accomplish what it ought to accomplish, it should include winter dairying. Cheese factories were confined for the summer months to the manufacture of cheese, and it was thought that a plant that permitted the manufacure of cheese in the summer and butter in the winter would be a more suitable one for the coming dairy day than any other single kind could possibly be, and this factory at Finch was constructed with that idea in mind. It is the intention to enlarge the operations of that factory by a small extension for the purpose of providing for the pasteurization of milk for the manufacture of cheese, and then we will be able to experiment and find out just how much pasteurization will improve the quality and see how far that one change will help us to regain our lost position in relation to the reception of our products in the British market.
We also intend to extend the testing system. In some provinces we have arranged for the testing locally by the provinces on the ground that they can do it more cheaply being right on the spot than we could do it from a common centre like Ottawa.
A growing industry like dairying always has some new activities and new expenses associated with it, necessitating a larger vote. We believe that there is no more complete food for human consumption than milk. It is nearer to being a perfect food than any other product, and we are endeavouring to develop a larger use of milk among our population both young and old. We have a lady, Miss Campbell, who has developed that work in an educational way, and in a very acceptable way, in various parts of the country, and she has an assistant at the present time. Possibly I might leave the matter now to the

committee to ask any questions they may have in mind rather than dealing with the subject generally.
Is Australia using the tuberculin test in the same way as Canada ?
I understand not.
It is depending on pasteurization?
I understand so.

Will anything be expended out of this appropriation for the establishment of a butter factory, say, in a new district where the people are anxious to go into the business? Could any of this vote be used for that purpose, and if so, in what way?

No. It is quite possible that in the near future we may construct another combined factory like the one at Finch, but that will not be decided upon until we know more definitely the results at the Finch factory. I think it is only a matter of time when we shall really want something like that in different parts of Canada. The construction of local factories such as my hon. friend refers to is a matter for the provincial government. I think my hon. friend is familiar with one in his constituency at a point called Fiske. The construction of that was assisted by the provincial department of agriculture in Saskatchewan, but any arrangement for assistance-with that exception,-has been invariably entered into by the provincial government.

When this question was before the committee several months ago I think there w'as a misunderstanding in regard to a number of items that were being discussed. I would ask the minister if this is the only item left in the estimates undisposed of?
This is the last item in the Main, Estimates. We have all of the estimates of civil government yet.

I may possibly be out of order in referring to any matter outside of this item but I should certainly like to ask the minister if any of these other items will be opened up for discussion. On the previous occasion referred to there was a misunderstanding and Hansard does not contain what is set forth in the Votes and Proceedings as to what actually took place. There is no reference whatever in Hansard to the item for the enforcement of the Agricultural Instruction Act. No reference whatever is made to that

item in Hansard and personally I did not hear the matter discussed in committee.

There is no Agricultural Instruction Act, but there is an agricultural instruction grant. The item is No. 50 "Administration of the agricultural instruction grant, $20,000". That has been passed. I may point out that if my hon. friend desires to discuss any question that has been passed my understanding is, he can do that on items of the estimates for civil government. If the committee desires to take up any question on any of these items I have no objection. I understand the usual practice is to do it on the civil government estimates when considerable latitude is allowed.
I think we had better have a clear understanding in that connection. I would like the chairman to endorse the minister's suggestion.

speechtext:

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The proceedings of
the House in committee are not only reported, but the Clerk makes a record of them and that record goes into the Votes and Proceedings which are open to every member. There have been complaints. I think the right hon. gentleman himself complained some time ago about Hansard incorrectly reporting him and giving him the credit for an address which he had never uttered, an address which was actually made by another member. The fact is that Hansard is not taken as the record in dealing with resolutions and items which come before the House. What is accepted is the report of the official who is appointed for that purpose under the rules of the House. The record he keeps is the one which is accepted and appears in the Votes and Proceedings.

If we accept the Chairman's statement then there is no record in Hansard at all, and a subject which should come up can be refused consideration. How it will be possible to rule otherwise I do not know. If with no record at all of the Hoppe discussion, no record whatever of the motion being made, and no recollection of it being made by any person in this House, we are going to be debarred from legitimate discussion here the sooner we know it the better.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I should just like to
draw the right hon. gentleman's attention to the fact that there is a record of the proceedings of the House signed by me and delivered to the Clerk, and the Clerk also signs the record. There is evidently a misunderstanding regarding the matter. Is the salary of the Commissioner of Agriculture ineluded in this item?

000.

Mr. Spencer: The minister has not answered my question :n regard to the salary of the Commissioner of Agriculture, Is that included in this item?

Mr. Chairman, such an appeal I am sure is irresistible. Besides, this is getting too quiet! But I want to assure the committee that I did not try to "put anything over" when they called out "earned". I am not going to stand in the way of discussing any vote.

speechtext: Does civil government stand?
The minister says it is passed.

I understand that when the estimates for civil government are under discussion, the salary of any employee of the government, whether included in the item or not, or anything pertaining to his appointment, may be discussed. I have been inquiring about that since then.

speechtext: The Chairman must accept the word of the minister as to whether an item comes under civil government unless it is clearly within his own knowledge. I assumed, quite naturally, that this matter did come within the item of civil government. I understand from the minister that the item of civil government has not yet passed, and the item is still open for debate.
Yes.

The fact is that the minister stated that it did come under civil government. This is included in another vote which passed after the chairman had given us the assurance that it came under civil government, and consequently we did not proceed to discuss it. We took his ruling that it came under civil government,, and subsequently the minister said we could have discussed it all right under the previous item which had just been passed, we having kept quiet abiding by the ruling of the chair.

The hon. member is making a mountain out of a mole hill. There is no disposition whatever to shut off discussion. If the committee wants to discuss it the present time is just as good as any other as far as I am concerned, but let us dc all things decently and in order. I thought at the time I made the statement that that was the proper procedure. I understood there was sufficient latitude under civil government, whether the name was there or not, to include any civil servant under any outside vote you desired to take him under, even

Supply-Agriculture-Dairying
though the vote might have been passed. I am not an authority on these matters, but that is my understanding.
You are usually right.

I was not present when the item was called, but I am very much interested in this vote, and I know that the minister has great zeal for the advancement of dairying; so much so that he sent one or two of the officials of his department to New Zealand within the last two months. Has the report from those officials been made to him, and will he have it printed and circulated, so that the members may have it?

I have an interim report that merely gives a survey of the ground covered, and does not come to any conclusions. It was a preliminary report that I asked for prior to the budget debate. The report which will include certain recommendations is being prepared, and I hope will be ready possibly in the course of a week. I would not like to state that absolutely. You never can tell. Sometimes it takes longer to do these things than we anticipate. But just as soon as possible it will be submitted to the House, and if an order is passed it will be printed and distributed.

Has the
minister any plans for the future looking towards putting into effect any recommendations that his officials may make?

Yes. I was sorry
that my hon. friend was out. One of them was with respect to the extension of the activities of the Finch factory, which is a combined factory for cheese and butter. We are enlarging that with the idea of providing for the pasteurization of milk for the manufacture of cheese. In the research in Australia and New Zealand, it was found that in those countries invariably the milk was pasteurized, and to that fact was attributed in some measure the high quality of their cheese. We are going to try that out in the Finch factory this summer, and then we shall be in a better position to know to what extent we can advise the construction of other large factories where it is deemed advisable throughout the country, especially in eastern Canada. We are satisfied that one of the reasons why the quality of our cheese has fallen behind is that it is made in a large number of small factories where the out-turn is so small and so varied, and where sometimes conditions are so primitive, that it is impossible to do justice to this industry.

We want to get a little more information about the Finch factory and pasteurization before we are able to say specifically just what kind of a standard factory would be suitable to conditions in Canada. I do not know whether we can get a standard or not, but we may get an approximate standard that can be varied to suit different localities.
Is the accommodation at Finch insufficient to take care of the milk that is being offered?

For the milk that is being offered now it is sufficient, but we have not accommodation for the pasteurization. That takes a little room itself and a pasteurization plant would have to be erected. Not very much of an extension will be required, but an extension will have to be made. After that we hope to enlarge the activities of the factory and to take on any milk that presents itself, to the full capacity of the factory.
If the accommodation is sufficient to look after the quantity of milk that is1 offered, will the minister explain why milk is being refused?

I did not quite
understand my hon. friend. It is sufficient to take on the patrons that are delivering milk, but it is not quite sufficient for all applicants. That is one of the reasons why we are enlarging it. I signed a statement yesterday or the day before intimating to the people in that vicinity that after we got this enlargement made, and beginning with the first of the new year, allcomers' milk would be accepted up to the full capacity of the factory, and regardless of where the milk came from. The factory is not sufficiently large to take care of allcomers, and to decide who was to be given preference and accommodated has been a rather awkward situation to deal with. There is only one policy to pursue, regardless of who is hurt and who is not. This is a demonstration factory to show that it is possible to make a high-class product at a low cost when the out-turn is large, and you cannot do that without hurting some of the little factories in the vicinity. It is about time that some of them were hurt-not wilfully, of course, but in a progressive movement of this nature some of the older institutions have to go by the board.

I approve
the minister's plans and I only hope he will carry out his good intentions.

I intend to do so.

Supply-Agriculture-Dairying

I know that in another branch of the department the minister is carrying on some work, and I must commend him for that also. That is in respect to grading of our dairy products for export. What progress is the minister making along that line?

I will state that very hurriedly because I have already gone over it. As my hon. friend knows, in the introduction of other reforms some objection is always raised. Possibly if we were to introduce a resolution that we were all to go to heaven to-night, somebody would object to it. No matter how admittedly good the grading system is, we had quite a number of, I will say, conscientious objectors to that system. My own view is that we should have had this about a quarter of a century ago, but these reforms sometimes come very slowly. Outside of a few localities the objection has not been serious, especially since the system has been put into actual practice and the benefits of it shown. I think the objection was largely raised because some people wanted to continue the old local activities of grading right near home, in the factory or in the car. There is a general antipathy to seeing your produce, instead of being handled in your own factories, sent down to a large factory at Montreal. You lose sight of it once it goes round the bend on the railway. Once the step is made the difficulty disappears; you wake up the next morning and you do not find very much difference. We hope, of course, to find a difference in the increased recognition of the product on the markets as a result of the grading. When the cheesemaker and the man who provides the raw material find they are paid on the basis of quality, they will have some inducement to furnish quality. I am glad that this commends itself to a practical dairyman like my hon. friend, and that he approves the Finch factory, which is a splendid plant, constructed some seven years ago, I think. I hope that under my administration we shall be able to carry out the expectations of the department in that regard. The factory at Finch is capable of splendid work, and the demonstration will be of exceeding value to the dairy industry of Ontario and, indeed, of the whole of Canada.

I noticed a short time ago that the Civil Service Commission sent out notices stating that ten dairy produce graders were required. Are these employed in connection with this work, and if so, at what points, in Ontario, at least, is the grading being carried on, in addition to Montreal?

When the Dairy Grading Act was passed a couple of years ago, it was decided not to put it into force. At the same time a number of dairy produce graders were appointed, and they started on voluntary grading of dairy produce at the new cold storage plant as soon as it was opened in Montreal. All the co-operative selling agencies as a rule patronize that cold storage plant at Montreal, and during the last year or year and a-half produce contributed voluntarily by the owners has been graded by these dairy graders. By introducing the system gradually in a voluntary way, we have been enabled to extend the usefulness of it and to demonstrate its usefulness to those who have been objecting. The work at Montreal has been substantially extended since 1st April, and in addition to that there are a number of graders in the vicinity of Belleville where there is a cold storage where cheese can be taken care of locally until they desire to export it. They operate from three or four places, taking Belleville as the centre. Wherever there is cold storage accommodation, where the cheese or butter can be kept at a proper temperature, the grading is done. It is not done at the factories because that would be impossible, for it would require an army of graders; it would be impossible to engage a grader for each of some eight hundred cheese factories in Ontario; that is out of the question. Besides, it is considered that such a system would not be satisfactory.

Does the minister mean to say that it would require a grader for each factory? Surely a grader could attend to twenty-five, thirty or forty factories. The conditions that would attend the grading at the factories were so obvious to many that, I fancy, the chief objection lay in that direction.
My hon. friend does, not advocate that, surely.

If the grading" were5 done at the factory the defects in the cheese could be pointed out to the maker. I know that the objection has been very strong in the past when the inspection has been made by the purchaser, at the factory. So far as western Ontario is concerned I do not think there was any serious complaint against the old system, but in eastern Ontario there was vigorous protest against adopting it. The minister says that the grading has been carried on at the cold storage plant at Montreal and also at Belleville. What about western Ontario and other points? The minister might also tell us what has been the success of the

Supply-Agriculture-Dairying
plant at Montreal. A very large cold storage plant has been constructed there, and the expense of operating it is very heavy, I should think. Can the minister tell us what the result has been so far, in the way of operating costs? And also what is being done in western Ontario? I should like to know, further, at what points grading is done.

The cold storage plant at Montreal is under the administration of the Harbour board. I had occasion to visit it last fall, when I went through it. It had been open less than a year and was three quarters filled and was doing good business. I suppose that it is now so well patronized as to be full all the time. That, however, is something I cannot speak about definitely; nor do I know what the revenues or the costs have been. As I say, it does not come under my department but under the Harbour board. I must say I admired the institution, and I believe it will fill a long-felt want; I should not be surprised if it were filled to capacity by this time. I gather from what my hon. friend says that he is half-disposed to favour the grading in the cheese factories. As a practical creamery man he must surely know that this would be impracticable. I do not need to enter into the reasons, one outstanding one being that, even taking one grader to two or three factories, you could not engage a large enough staff of them to cover all the factories. And in any case, the grading can be better done in the way proposed. So far as western Ontario is concerned, London is one of the centres, and the work is being done as requirements demand.
