speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When the committee
rose at six o'clock, item 42, page 21 of the Estimates, was under consideration. Shall the resolution carry?
I was not in the chamber when the committee rose. Will the minister state briefly what this item covers?

As British Columbia is rapidly becoming a dairy province and has acquired some fame by producing a cow that has made a world record, perhaps a few moments devoted to an explanation of this item may not be out of place, even if I have to indulge in a little repetition. In a general way, dairying is becoming of more importance
[Mr Sutherland.]
to agriculture throughout Canada as time goes on. Some years ago it was looked upon as confined entirely to eastern Canada, but as the western provinces have found some form of diversification necessary they have seriously taken up dairying, even in the prairie provinces, where it had not been looked upon with very much favour. In British Columbia, because of the high cost of dairy products, the people have been encouraged to go into it to the full capacity of their pasture and of their feed. This involves additional expense in, the way of educational work, cow testing, the new system of grading, and so on. That, in a general way, is what the vote is for: more money and a larger staff are required for the purposes of administration.
I assume that under this item the expenses of Mr. Duncan Marshall will be paid in connection with his trip to the Old Country. Just what are his duties there at the present time?

If my hon. friend will be satisfied, I suggest that as soon as we pass this vote and take up civil government, there will be an opportunity to discuss Mr. Marshall from any aspect that may be deemed in the public interest. He is not paid out of this vote; it would be irregular to enter upon that discussion now, and I think that these proprieties ought to be observed. If that would be agreeable to the committee as a whole, I am sure it will be agreeable to me.

The minister is unnecessarily alarmed; he is exceedingly sensitive. I was going to make a very ipnocent inquiry, and I think about two minutes would have satisfied me. I have no bone to pick, nor have I any particular criticism to offer; I was a humble seeker of a little further information. But the minister bristles up; he seems to sense a serious attack of something of the kind. Why, I am the last person ip the world, he ought to know, to precipitate anything of that kind. But either Mr. Marshall or someone else is in the Old Country picking up some thoroughbred stock with the idea of improving Canadian herds. I myself am interested in farming; I would like to know just what the department is doing, and certainly that comes under this item of dairying. I am not particularly interested ip Mr. Marshall's salary; in fact, I think I know what it is; it is reported to be $6,000. So that the minster need not worry about the civil government item so far as I am concerned.

My hon. friend is probably thinking of Mr. Archibald, who went

Supply-Agriculture-Dairying
over there during the winter months and brought back some valuable pure-bred cattle, hogs and sheep. That comes under the experimental farm vote. Now, sin,ce my hon. friend is in an amiable frame of mind, and I am myself, if the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) feels similarly disposed, I do not care whether it is on this vote or on another that Duncan Marshall is discussed.
I may add, however, that we discussed the subject for something like three-quarters of an hour before six o'clock, and I did not know whether my hon. friend was merely continuing it until the arrival of reinforcements.

Again my hon. friend is frightfully sensitive on this subject. I have not spoken to any of my colleagues about the matter. It just shows how correct we must be -how our minds must run along the same channel.
Well, I myself want to fit in with that desirable state of mind.

It would be very difficult for the minister to fit into the groove he would find here. But it just shows there must be something in the back of his mind, a sort of subconscious sense of guilt which he does not like to admit. There must be a feeling on his part that he did not do exactly the right thing in appointing Mr. Marshall; that perhaps it was his personal desire as well as the interest of Mr. Marshall, that dictated the appointment. The circumstance arouses suspicion even in my mind, which I am sure my hon. friend will admit is usually free from such things. Still, the minister has not answered my question about what Mr. Marshall is doing in the Old Country. That is all I want to know.

If I am in order, Mr. Chairman, in replying to such an eminently respectable question put in such a very nice spirit, I shall be delighted to do so. Mr. Marshall has just completed negotiations with respect to the removal of the embargo on breeding cattle, and at the request of the Duke of Devonshire that question has been suspended until the meeting of the Imperial Conference in London this fall He has been instructed to superintend in the meantime the arrival of a shipment of chilled beef which is being sent by this department from Montreal, and to compare the values of cattle slaughtered on this side and sent over in the form of chilled beef as against cattle slaughtered immediately on arrival in England, and as against another bunch that will be sent over and sold for
Stockers; that is, he is going to compare values in three different sales, cattle slaughtered on arrival, cattle slaughtered on this side and sent over in the form of chilled beef, and cattle sold for stockers. Mr. Marshall has been asked to remain there and superintend this shipment, to inspect it, and note the condition in which it arrives and how it is received on the market, because it is an entirely new work so far as we are concerned. Something of a similar nature was conducted by the Harris Abattoir Company this year, but what we know ourselves we will know, and we thought it advisable at this time to conduct such an experiment entirely under the supervision of our own experimental farm system, with a representative in Great Britain to report on all the details. That is what he is doing at the present time. The cattle will arrive there in about a week. Previously he had been reporting on the arrivals of the stockers. There has been some difficulty in Great Britain with regard to the classification of our cattle, the British government taking the ground that a lot of these animals ought not to be classified as stockers but as fat cattle, and that they should be slaughtered immediately on arrival. There has also been some difficulty as to what ports are eligible for the slaughter of these cattle on arrival, whether it should be Birkenhead or Glasgow, or both. These are matters that Mr. Marshall is looking after at the present time with the British authorities pending the arrival of this shipment. After that is over he is returning to Canada as there is nothing further to be done in regard to the embargo until the Imperial Conference this fall.

Does not the minister think it would be advisable to keep a permanent official in England to superintend our shipments of cattle and of chilled beef with a view to protecting the Canadian shipper and his market in Great Britain? I do not think we should take what they say in England. We should have some competent official permanently stationed there who would inspect all cattle on arrival, and I would like to know if the Minister of Agriculture has such a step in contemplation.

There is only one primary complaint I have against the Civil Service Commission-and as a matter of fact it is not against them at all, but against the act by which they are governed and must be governed, the act by which we are all governed-and that is the desperate, interminable time it takes to get an appointment through. We only pass through this world once, and we want to live while we are living. We do not want to make these appointments in eternity but to make them in time to have the men to do the work.

of a trip to South America to develop the live stock industry as between Canada and South America. Consequently the activities of Mr. Marshall since that time and down to the present have been in the public eye more or less. At that time I believe he was passing the winter at a seaside resort in Florida, and some inquiries were made upon that occasion with regard to his activities there. I believe the minister intimated that he had been loaned for the time being to the Minister of the Interior to promote immigration to this country, and he was delivering some very effective addresses in Florida during the winter. Early in the present session I made inquiries as to the result of his operations there, and I was informed that no apparent results had been secured, or at least that there had been no immigration from Florida to Canada so far as was known. Mr. Duncan Marshall was in the public eye at that time by reason of the fact that his appointment had been made not by the Civil Service Commission but by order in council. Immediately upon the prorogation of parliament, in fact, the very day that parliament prorogued, Mr. Marshall landed in the constituency that I represent and on that day he addressed a gathering of the Liberals of that constituency, and had a very enjoyable time, I have no doubt. I have no fault to find with Mr. Marshall appearing at a gathering of the Liberals of South Oxford or of any other constituency, but so long as he is being paid by the people of this country to perform certain duties I think it is well that he should attend to those duties and not devote his time to political matters.

That is what we had in mind. It was about the blackest outlook that
wr had for our cattle for the last thirty years, and I could not find then, nor am I able to find yet, a more competent man for that kind of work than Duncan Marshall. Now, as to that I may be mistaken; we all have our opinions about the competency or fitness of men. The fact that he and Dr. Grisdale, accompaning two of my colleagues to England last autumn, succeeded in terminating the embargo should at least be some indication of the value of his work in connection with this line of activity.

Yes, that is something like the claims that are set up in connection with the winning of the war. As my hon. friend knows a good many countries claim the credit for winning the war. I have said on several occasions here that as far as I was concerned I was willing to distribute any credit that was coming among the public men who were identified with the movement for the elimination of this embargo, and there is some credit coming to Manning Doherty and also to the right hon. leader of the Opposition and his colleagues.
Mr. Drury claimed all the credit, I notice.
Mr. Drury possibly requires all the arguments he can muster.
Oh probably; I will agree with that.
I have a very warm feeling for Mr. Manning Doherty and may- [DOT] be there was necessity for provincial activity at that time. A quick, short stroke sometimes does the trick.

As to the work for
which Mr. Marshall and Mr. Dryden were employed, I believe the committee were led to understand that in addition to the beef breeds the pure-bred dairy stock were also to be taken under consideration. clearly shown that the administration of the Agricultural Instruction Act is largely connected with dairying in Ontario. This is the order in council in question:
The Committee of the Privy Council have had before them a report, dated 1st February, 1922, from the Minister of Agriculture, submitting that the Agricultural Instruction Act under which the sum of $1,100,000 annually has been granted to the Provincial Departments of Agriculture for the purpose of aiding agricultural instruction in the provinces expires March 31st, 1923.
The minister states that in view of the extraordinary and exceptional conditions in the agricultural world it is highly desirable that an investigation be made into the advisability of the continuation, discontinuation or emendation of the provisions of this act; the amounts to be paid, and the methods of calculating such amounts in the event of its extension; and the scope of the work of the provinces to be undertaken with the assistance of funds provided thereunder.
It is considered advisable that a commissioner be appointed under section 38c of the Civil Service Act as amended by chapter 22 of the Statutes of 1921, to conduct the investigation indicated above, and to inquire into such other agricultural problems as may be desirable and necessary.
The minister, therefore, recommends that Mr. Duncan Marshall, of Olds, Alberta, be appointed as a commissioner for the above purpose, and to perform such other duties of a cognate nature as may be delegated to him.
The minister further recommends that Mr. Marshall be paid a salary at the rate of $6,000 per annum, said salary to be paid from the appropriation provided for the administration of the Agricultural Instruction Act and that this appointment date from January 15, 1922.
The committee concur in the foregoing recommendations and submit the same for approval.

I have here a booklet, "Dairy Produce Act and Regulations Administered by the Dairy and Cold Storage Branch." On page 9, I read:
The owner of the cheese or butter shall arrange in a suitable place and open all boxes or packages for inspection.
This has to do with the grading of cheese and butter. I would like an explanation of that regulation, in view of these conditions. In our district we have at least two cheese factories from which butter is shipped direct to Scotland; nobody sends to Montreal or any of these grading points, and it would certainly be inconvenient for the owner, or any employee connected with that factory to go to the point of grading. What shall be done under those circumstances?

It will depend upon who the consignee is. Very little of this produce is sent on what we call consignment. It has to be purchased first and the consignee sends it to whatever cold storage plant is most convenient to him for the purpose of grading. He cannot grade it without exposing it. This provision, as my hon. friend knows, is just in its second month; I have been asking my staff as to how it is working, and I understand it is working quite smoothly. If my hon. friend knows of any hitch in the matter, I should be very pleased to hear about it. No doubt in the introducing of an entirely new law like this some little difficulties will arise, but we will be very pleased to iron them out. What is the particular difficulty he has in mind?

I quite understand that in the working out of a new regulation like this there will be some difficulty. The cheese factories referred to are in Peterborough county and my attention was drawn to this by the owner of one of these factories. I undertsand there is an arrangement by which the season's make is sold direct to a dealer in Scotland at a price in advance of the local price.

No consignee can send cheese or butter without having it previously graded. One of the terms of the act provides that both must be graded. When I was in the cold storage plant last autumn in Montreal the graders were at work there. Obviously each parcel has to be exposed before the graders can get at it, with their stick or auger, and it is closed up after the grading is done.
In view of the section which says that the owner or some person appointed by him shall open the boxes, how would you regulate such a condition as I have referred to?

You will have some person there representing you. Suppose you want to send a consignment to Montreal, you must send it to some person who can perform the service for you. This paragraph says that the owner of the cheese or butter shall arrange in a suitable place, and so on. It may be in Montreal, Belleville, London or some other place. It is the privilege of the party owning the cheese to have it examined wherever he likes. The hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) seemed to be under the impression that we stipulated where the parcels of dairy produce would be examined. That is a matter for the owners of the produce to determine, they notify the government, and wherever the produce is sent we do the grading. If it happens to be in Montreal, we have a staff at Montreal to attend to it, because there is a great deal of produce going there. In other places the graders move about wherever cheese or butter is being sent. We have had that system in vogue in Saskatchewan for many years. Wherever there is a cold storage the produce can be graded. It is necessary to have a cold storage, because you cannot keep butter or cheese to-day without a cold storage plant. We had no difficulty under our system; we were notified by the owners of the butter in the West when they wanted it graded, and we would send a man to do the grading wherever the produce was located, Saskatoon, Battleford, Prince Albert, or Melfort-wherever it was desired. It is the same here. If you cannot go yourself, there is a man who will handle these matters with regard to inspection and then close them up.

I would like to know if the minister has in mind any new dairy policy that he intends to bring down at an early date, with a view to improving dairy conditions, increasing our output and getting a better share

of the British market in the near future. In 1880, we exported about nineteen million pounds of butter. During the same year the little country of Denmark with three million people exported about twenty-seven million pounds of butter. In 1921, our export had shrunk to nine million pounds and the Danish output had increased to a hundred and ninety-nine million pounds. As all hon. members know, we produce all our grain and concentrates within our own country. Our conditions for producing this grain are, perhaps, second to none, while the Danes import a great deal of concentrates from other countries, particularly from the United States and Canada. Apparently there must be something wrong with the dairy industry in this country with a population of nine million people and millions of acres of land as compared with the very small country of Denmark with a population of only three million. Perhaps some of our oleo friends will say that this is due to our having oleo manufactured in this country since 1918. As a matter of fact, the Danes introduced oleomargarine factories in 1882, and they have been manufacturing oleomargarine in that country ever since that time, with the result that during the past year they ate forty-eight pounds of oleomargaine per capita of their population, while we were carefully protected against oleomargarine prior to 1918. Therefore, that cannot be the cause of the backwardness of the dairy industry in Canada. Is it due to the quality of the product? The Danish cow produces 160 pounds of butter fat per annum as compared with about 125 pounds produced by the Canadian cow. I understand that our products are not received with as great favour as the Danish products in the British market on account of lack of flavour, keeping quality and colour. Is that due to poor grading on this side or to better grading in Denmark? These all appear to be questions that should receive the careful attention of the government at an early date, because this is one branch of agriculture that should be developed to its greatest possibilities. We, I understand, are supplying only a very small proportion of the butter consumed in Great Britain and imported from outside points. Has the minister any new policy in view to meet this situation?

Only the importance of the work and the interest that my hon. friend has taken in it, both combined, tempt me to go over some of the same ground that I have gone over now two or three times; but as I said before, possibly it will bear repeating. I have discussed already at some length.

Supply-Agriculture-Dairying
at the request of various hon. gentlemen as they have arrived in the committee, certain phases of this subject, but there are a number of matters to which my hon. friend has referred that have not yet been taken up. So I am sure he will excuse me if I confine my remarks to those new problems to which he so properly refers.
One of the works we intend to take up is the establishment of a research laboratory. 1 do not think I have referred to that before during this session. Some hon. members will remember the excess acidity and bacteria that were found in some of our cheese in the British market. This created quite a stir there, and the cheese was traced back to the factory in which it was made. We were not, however, able to locate the bacteria. That teaches us that we have a great deal to learn about acidity and bacteria in cheese. In that cheese there was evidently some bacteria that was noxious to public health because it caused sickness, and a few incidents like that might seriously affect the standing of our cheese. Fortunately this did not occur because there was only one incident of this kind. We have $20,000 set down for the establishment of that laboratorjr. Nobody in this House knows better than the hon. member for Victoria City (Mr. Tolmie) the importance of research work, either along the lines of veterinary practice, or, as I intimated, in connection with this creamery work.
In order that we may be able to report quickly back to the Department of Agriculture the condition particularly of our dairy products as they arrive in Great Britain, it is proposed, if my colleagues and also the Civil Service Commission are agreeable, to appoint a representative in Great Britain for the purpose of looking after the condition of our dairy products on their arrival there, to see that they get proper recognition and proper advertising, and to report back any defects so that we may remedy them at the earliest possible moment. During the war a certain amount of carelessness was discoverable, not only in Canada but in all other countries, with respect to the condition of farm produce. Because of the urgent demand, everything in the form of fats went. A hog was a hog. To some extent the same conditions applied to butter. During those years the quality of our labour deteriorated, and this had its effect on the quality of our produce. Now we have to pull up. New Zealand and Australia are making remarkable strides towards improvement. The size of their factories, their large turnover, their large herds, render them capable of getting
good managers and paying them good salaries, thus enabling them to produce a high class quality. They are able to make this business more or less of a specialty, just as we in this country make a specialty of growing wheat, although that is no reason why we should not diversify our interests. They make a specialty of dairy products; they put their whole thought into the business ; they are prepared to submit to almost any kind of governmental supervision or restriction in order that they may get the best results possible. Because of that they have surpassed us in quality, and as regards dairy produce we have encountered competition that we have never before experienced in the history of Canada. We must do our utmost in order to meet that competition. We must develop that Finch factory with which my hon. friend is familiar, enlarge it and make accommodation in it for pasteurizing milk, for that is one of the reasons why they are able to make such high class cheese in Australia and New Zealand. We are extending that factory for that purpose, and at the end of another year we shall be able to know just what will be the value of a larger factory to the dairy industry of Canada as it has proved so advantageous to the dairy industries in our sister dominions.
Another matter is the importance of testing out our cows, the development of the testing system, weeding out the scrubs-that is what this means-weeding out what we familiarly call the boarders. The average man with a bunch, say, of ten or twelve cows, if half of them are poor, will find that it takes the good ones to carry the poor ones, and at the end of the year he will be about where he began. It is only by the use of the scales that you really can realize the difference between a good testing cow and a poor one. That work will be carried on with greater activity than ever, because the very first requisite to successful dairying is to get the proper kind of cows. If you do not do that, all your subsequent activities are of little avail.
I think I have covered most of the questions which my hon. friend raised. There is one more matter to which I might refer, and which I am sure the committee will be interested in. The butter we are making now in eastern Canada is largely produced for home consumption; it is salted to suit home consumption, and that does not suit the taste of the British market. Out in the West we have started a system of grading and manufacturing largely with the object of suiting the British Columbia taste. The British Columbia taste is very much the British taste, and so the farmers and dairymen in the West

Supply-Agriculture-Dairying
have been trained to produce a butter that will also meet the requirements of the British market. The three prairie provinces have taken the initial step in the exporting of products direct to the United Kingdom. The butter is graded out there, and an arrangement has been made between the Dominion and the provincial graders whereby the provincial grading is accepted. I believe it is a good grading, because it was established on the same basis as the Dominion grading; and the creameries being larger units with a more uniform turnout, they found last year that the shipments from the West brought five shillings per long hundred more than any eastern butter. By making large export shipments from the West, where we have adopted that grading system, we can relieve the pressure on eastern butter, a great deal of which was shipped formerly, and can send the butter from the West direct to the British market. In this way we can hold our home market for eastern butter and thus maintain our reputation at a high standard. I do not know that it is anybody's fault that butter has fallen away in eastern Canada. The fact is attributable, I believe, partly to war conditions and partly to the circumstance that the quality demanded for home consumption is different from that of the British market.
Is it not a fact that the British market demands butter that contains less salt than butter intended for Canadian consumption?
Surely; and the bulk of the New Zealand butter is shipped without any salt at all, or at least with very little.
Is not that the main reason why eastern Canadian butter is not in demand in the British market?
That is partly the reason.
It is not because of the poor quality of eastern Canadian butter, but because it contains too much salt for the British taste.

It is due in part also to a dividing of interests between butter and cheese; my hon. friend (Mr. Caldwell), I think, knows what the reason is. It is due to the fact that a lot of cream is over ripe or over fermented, whichever you like, before it gets to many of the central creameries in Ontario, and that tends to injure the whole reputation of the country. We have a cool climate in the West, and while sometimes coolers are not an advantage

in midwinter, nevertheless our cool nights are a decided advantage to dairying in that part of the country. Besides that, there is the fact that we have nothing to unlearn. Not long ago we were starting at the bottom of the ladder in dairying and, without anything to unlearn, we adopted proper grading methods at the very outset. It is far easier to start right than to get right after you have been forty years wrong; and that is the condition of affairs in the West. I say that, of course, absolutely without any disparagement of eastern Canada. The dairymen in that part of the country have been satisfying the requirements they have had to meet, and that is all that any dairyman can be expected to do. The export was small while the home demand was large, and there is no kick from the consumers in eastern Canada. But there is an old saying, that what is one man's meat is another man's poison, and butter that suits the taste of eastern Canada is not suitable to the British market.
Now you are on safer ground.

Possibly; but we were trained in the West to fill the market of British Columbia in competition with New Zealand, and the taste of British Columbia in this matter is that of the British market. The result is that the British Columbia market is now very largely filled by local supplies, except at certain times of the year. Our aim is to ship co-operatively direct right through to the British market with a view to getting the highest possible return for our produce; and, at least for the time being, until the dairymen can get more assistance, for the further purpose of stemming the downward tendency of our butter in comparison with other countries.
What proportion of our export butter is pasteurized?

Nearly all the
prairie butter is pasteurized, and that makes a great difference in its keeping qualities. We began out there without any pasteurization. I went up to the manager of the Cooperative Creameries of British Columbia shortly after our activities began, and visited the wholesale dealers in Vancouver, to find out what kind of butter they had. I wanted to know whether the taste of the people was in any way finical, or whether it was just like that of ordinary people. But whatever it was, the idea was to produce an article that would satisfy it. There is no use undertaking to educate people to a different taste; if you can meet their demand that is the

Supply-Agriculture-Dairying
wisest thing to do. I discovered that what they wanted was a mildly salted butter, and that is what they have been supplied
9 p.m. with. Our produce dealers have all been strongly advised to establish pasteurizing plants in connection with every creamery in the province, and that policy has been put into force. I do not know whether it has been completed yet or not, but in every factory of any size I believe that such a plant has been established, because it is absolutely necessary to preserve the keeping properties of butter. Furthermore, it is necessary in the manufacture of cheese.
Has the cheapness of salt, as compared with the price of butter, anything to do with the super-salting of our butter?
Just a trifle.

I rather object to that, because I do not think that the fact that our butter is not in larger demand in the British market is due so much to the poor quality as to the fact that we put a good deal of salt into it.

The salt does not cost nearly as much as butter and it does not do any harm to salt it, with weight in view. But under our new act I do not think that anyone will be able to put more than 4 per cent of salt into his butter, so that there will be a limitation in that direction anyhow. On that point, however, I think there is a great difference in the kind of salt that is used. It is very important that the best salt be put into butter, and we have found that the Australians have undoubtedly discovered the right kind of salt that is necessary. That, however, is a commercial question which I think it would be well for us to refrain from discussing.

In a discussion that occurred some time ago we heard a good deal about hogs contracting cholera from feeding on whey. I want to ask the minister this question: If whey will give disease to hogs, does it follow that the cheese or the butter manufactured from the same milk would be affected?
That is an open question. So far as tuberculosis is concerned, it might, but I do not know about cholera.
I have in mind any disease at all.

The whey in factories has been pasteurized right along to kill all germs in it so that there might be eliminated any risk of contagion to the animals that fed on it. That is one of the arguments why you might as well pasteurize milk in the first instance as to pasteurize the whey afterwards.
The minister does not catch the point. If the whey is affected, does it follow that the cheese or butter manufactured from the milk itself is likely to be affected too?
The hon. member means, I suppose, if it is unpasteurized?
Yes.

Oh, well, as regards unpasteurized milk, I do not care whether it is from an accredited herd or not, there is always a certain amount of danger to be feared, because you cannot keep continually testing it, and there is a time in the interval between tests when tuberculosis will manifest itself. When the milk is tested, of course, the risk is reduced to the minimum. We sometimes hear of certified milk being advertised. I do not think there is any such thing unless accreditation is supplemented by pasteurization. If you have unpasteurized milk in the case of cheese, or unpasteurized cream in the case of butter, there is danger of the tuberculosis being passed on to the butter. As a matter of fact it is bacterial action in the butter after it is made that conduces to its non-keeping properties. There is no question that there is a certain element of danger of communication of the tuberculosis; the only absolutely safe way, in the case of either milk or cream, is to keep the herds as clean as possible by testing, and to supplement that by pasteurization. The very best authorities in the world hold that view.

There is no question about the possibility of butter from tubercular cows, particularly cows with infected udders, being infected with tuberculosis. It seems to be an entirely wrong policy to pasteurize the whey or the buttermilk and feed it to the hogs, and not to employ pasteurization in the case of the butter consumed by the people. That is one important feature of the dairying industry that might be carefully looked into with a view to making progress along these lines. The result would be not only to improve the keeping qualities of our dairy products, but also to protect human beings from the ravages of tuberculosis. It has been shown in our packing houses that in recent years the percentage of hogs infected with tuberculosis has increased from about 10 to 22 per cent in a very short time. It is a fact also that hogs affected with tuberculosis have come to

Supply-Agriculture-Dairying
the packing houses in largest numbers from those districts where dairying is carried on and where they are raised on the dairy by-products showing clearly that tuberculosis is transmitted by these products without any difficulty whatever. By carrying on pasteurization we are taking a decided step toward the eradication of tuberculosis, particularly in the hogs of this country.

The minister made a remark with regard to certified milk. What
guarantee does certified milk carry?
It certifies that the cows from which the milk is drawn are free from tuberculosis.

I understood the
minister to say that that was worth nothing if the milk was not pasteurized.

No; I said there
was no absolute certainty about it, for this reason: The period between tests is usually about six months. We will say there is a herd of five cows; they are all tested and there is no reaction. Six months elapse, and upon testing there is found to be one reactor. From the day in that six months' period when that animal became a reactor, up to the time of the second test, milk has been taken from a tubercular cow. There is not very much chance during that period of clinical symptoms developing, and there is not much chance of infection, but there is some; therefore, I do not think we are safe in looking upon any raw milk as absolutely sure; the only way to make sure is to pasteurize it.
Does the minister assure us that pasteurization is a guarantee against tuberculosis?
Yes, if it is properly done. Pasteurization, like anything else, can be improperly done.
Does the minister mean that it is a 100 per cent guarantee? If so, at what temperature is the pasteurization carried on?

At an average, in this country, of about 150 degrees Fahrenheit. That is looked upon as the correct temperature, provided you maintain it long enough; if it is just flashed on carelessly and then flashed off, there will not be time to permit permeation of the whole of the product. The temperature should be maintained for at least twenty minutes; half an hour is safer. Our representatives who were recently in New Zealand brought back the information that in that, country they pasteurize at a much higher

temperature than we use-165 degrees or more. If they are right, then we can make assurance doubly sure by getting up to the maximum temperature that can be attained without destroying the food properties of the article. I understand that a temperature of even as high as 200 degrees can be employed.
What is the highest temperature that can be applied without seriously flavouring the product?

I think that is one of the things in connection with which our research men will bring out some further information. But the fact is that in New Zealand they run from 30 to 40 degrees higher than we do, and turn out a much better product. The fact that New Zealand and Australia stand first in the world in the matter of butter is an indication that the flavour of the product is not injured by the high temperature employed in pasteurization.

Is it the opinion of the
minister's experts that the New Zealand butter for export is of better quality, and better flavour, than good Canadian butter?
Yes, they are quite satisfied that New Zealand has the "edge" on Canada so far as the quality of butter is concerned.

Out in British Columbia we do not admit that. We think the fresh Canadian product, made in our creamery where the cream is carefully graded, is much better in flavour than the New Zealand butter, -and we are constantly in competition with the New Zealand product on the coast.

Of course, tastes
can be cultivated. The British market prefers butter made of sweet cream, and not too highly salted; that is their conception of what is good butter. Now, in New Zealand they pasture their cattle outside the whole year round, and everyone knows that it is easier to make good butter out of stabling season than during stabling season, so that they have an advantage in that respect. After all, it is uniformity the year round that is required, and a constant supply on the market. The question has been asked out in the prairies: "If we all go into dairying, if we all go into butter making, is it going to be the old story that as soon as we have something to sell the prices drop?" I assure the committee that not only do you require a good article on the British market in competition with the world, but you require to have that article on the market the year round. The

Supply-Agriculture-Dairying
customer does not want to go to a retailer to-day, ask for Canadian butter and get it, and then find the next day that he cannot be supplied. The people want to know what they are getting and they want to be able to get it when they want it. If we have butter on that market part of the year and none the rest of the year, we shall never get a proper grip on the market. Last year we supplied 2J per cent of the butter imports of the British people; we send them two and half pounds out of every hundred that they import. Under these circumstances the more butter we make in the lifetime of this generation the better position we will occupy on the British market because of the continuity of supply that we shall keep there.

With reference to a statement of the minister a few moments ago regarding the gratifying of the British palate in the matter of butter, I heard a statement with regard to Canadian pork by a noted authority who had just returned from Britain. He said that the reason for the preference for Irish and Danish bacon was also largely a matter of salting. I would like the minister to investigate that.
That is correct. They are so close to Britain that they can send their products over with very mild salting, and very often with no salting at all. In addition, they do not use saltpetre.

In regard to what the minister has said with regard to the tuberculin test, I should like to ask him what good he thinks this large amount of money that is being spent on the test at the present time is doing to the agricultural portion' of this country and to the people at large.

I think it is doing incalculable good. If there was no check on the disease it would get worse and worse all the time. It is not in the incipient stages that there is very much danger, but only when it reaches the stage when there is a reaction to the test that there is risk to the human family from the milk. Take Great Britain herself, I think her cattle run about forty per cent tubercular. Their proportion is very much higher than ours at all events. Any country that neglects the testing will certainly soon find her animals pretty well honey-combed with tuberculosis, especially where there is so much stabling to be done as in Canada. It is a stable disease just as tuberculosis in the human family is a house disease. While I do not think the last word has been said with respect to the best test
obtainable, for I think science will yet discover something better than the tuberculin test, it is the best thing in sight at the present time, and until we get a better I think we should continue using it.

I quite agree with the minister that there is an object to be gained, but this hit-and-miss game we are playing at the present time is to my mind of very little use to the country at large. There is no endeavour to make it complete in any one part of the country, and there is consequently no advantage to the man who submits his herds to the tuberculin test, because his milk is mixed with the milk of other men who have not had the test made, and in that way the public has no guarantee that the milk is free from disease. There are only a few people in this country who have been able to get the benefit of these tuberculin tests, and I can see but little good to be derived from the amount of money spent on the test so long as it is not made general. I quite agree that if it was made general we could gain something, but as it is now we are not gaining anything. You might just as well not make the test as let the milk from cows that have been tested be mixed with that of cows that have not been tested, because there is no guarantee at all as to the purity of the milk. There is no protection against tuberculosis in such a system, and the campaign at present being carried on is to my mind of little use tc this country.

I think we are a little beside the mark. Possibly my hon. friend was not in when we were dealing with the vote under the Health of Animals branch. I draw his attention to it in order that we may get some information along the lines he has suggested. We have applied the tuberculin test in three municipalities in Manitoba. We have tested every bovine animal in those three municipalities, and have found that they run about five per cent tubercular. The idea is to get some information as to what it is going to cost. It is going to mean a big cost and when the public is prepared for a campaign of that nature, by undertaking this work we shall have the information as to what it is going to cost. I have pointed out that possibly we shall be able to get public sentiment sufficiently active that the federal and provincial authorities and possibly the larger municipalities will join hands in a campaign such as my hon. friend suggests, but it is going to cost something, and it is well to know the cost before we start out



Supply-Agriculture-Dairying
I was in when that discussion was on. I Should like to know how soon a campaign of that nature will be conducted.
I do not know. It will depend on public sentiment.
It should be more than public sentiment.

I appreciate the difficulty in proceeding with the testing of all the herds in the country at one time. As the minister states, it would be a very expensive work. It seems remarkable that there should be an effort made to eradicate disease from the pure-bred herds while the dairy herds that are supplying milk for human consumption are not receiving the same attention. In the two or three municipalities referred to in the province of Manitoba you may be able to show what can be done by taking a whole section and subjecting it to this test, but there are undoubtedly great difficulties to be met with by reason of the fact that people are constantly buying and selling and there is a mixture of the healthy animals with those that are not free from the disease.
To my mind one of the greatest dangers that we have to-day is the great increase in tuberculosis in the swine of this country. It is really startling to those who are engaged in the business to realize the prevalence of tuberculosis among swine, and I believe it is very largely the result of their consuming dairy products. If anything can be done by pasteurization of the products to remove this menace I think it should be done.
With regard to New Zealand the minister has stated that the high quality of New Zealand butter is so apparent that it is noticeable to every one. I notice that dairy cattle in New Zealand run out the year round or are practically grazing the year round, and consequently I do not suppose they would be subject to anything like the same degree of tuberculosis as Canadian cattle, which are stabled for six and often eight months in the year, and very often in unsanitary stables which must be conducive to breeding this disease. While you may eradicate the disease from a herd, in order to keep the herd free from disease, it is absolutely essential that sanitary conditions should prevail in the stables, otherwise the disease will break out again and conditions will be nearly as bad as before. It is such a big problem under present conditions that I realize how difficult it is for the minister to proceed with the work as rapidly as he would like, but I think that 
the herds which are supplying milk for human consumption should receive a little more attention than they are receiving at the present time.

Could the minister inform the House as to the percentage of those animals which do not show disease after having been condemned for slaughter. There must be a record kept of the animals that are free from the disease, and it would be interesting to show the accuracy of the test. There is a suspicion in the minds of a great many people that the test is not a very reliable one. If it were generally understood that the test was-I will not say infallible, but as nearly so as possible, it would remove a suspicion in the minds of many people.

Reports indicate
that the amount of infection runs from the undiscoverable lesion up to the state where the inside of the animal is covered with tubercules the size of a pea. There may also be tubercules in the liver. They are found largely in the viscera. Under healthy conditions the tubercule becomes encysted; it is surrounded with a fleshy growth. It is sealed in there, and nature, under the most healthy conditions, takes care of it. That tubercule will be sufficient to make the animal re-act although it may be in perfect looking health. I do not want to dilate too much on the system but it is the best we have got yet. I think the percentage where the disease is not at all apparent to the naked eye is somewhere between 6 and 8 per cent- 1 think about 8 per cent. It may be there to an extent sufficient to cause a reaction and yet not sufficient to form into actual pustules or little tubercules.
Could the minister tell us how many herds were under the accredited herd system three years ago and how many now?
There are about 700 herds all over Canada now. I read out the number for each province.
Is that fully accredited?
Those are the fully accerdited herds, and then there are about 500 in the various stages.
Could you tell us how many there were two or three years ago?
None three years ago.

I have taken occasion to look into the question of the power of the government to make the appointment of Mr. Duncan Marshall since I was informed tonight by the minister as to the methods they devised to do it in order to get around the provisions of the Civil Service Act. Now I commence with this assertion: The government's appointment of Mr. Duncan Marshall is plainly, obviously and brazenly illegal. They had no power to appoint him whatsoever. I have before me the order in council under which the appointment to-day exists. It was passed on the 7th of February, 1922, not long after the government came into office, just long enough, I presume for the importunities of Mr. Marshall to have reached their full height. The minister recites in his recommendation to council that parliament has set aside $1,100,000 for the purposes of the Agricultural Instruction Act. Then he proceeds to indicate the plan by which that sum can be invaded and turned over, in part, to Mr. Duncan Marshall. Let me quote the language of the order in council :
The minister states that in view of the extraordinary and exceptional conditions in the agricultural world-
I presume that instability in Europe that required the Minister of Finance's statement as to the vital necessity of stability in our tariff to hold it steady-
-it is highly desirable that an investigation Ibe made into the advisability of the continuation, discontinuation, or emendation of the provisions of this act; $he amounts to be paid, and the methods of calculating such amounts in the event of its extension; and the scope of the work of the provinces to be undertaken with the. assistance of funds provided thereunder.
It is considered advisable that a commissioner her appointed under section 38c of the Civil Service Act as amended by chapter 22 of the statutes of 1921, to conduct the investigation indicated above, and to inquire into such other agricultural problems as may be desirable and necessary.
The minister therefore recommends that Mr. Duncan Marshall, of Olds, Alberta, be appointed as a commissioner for the above purpose and to perform such other duties of a cognate nature as may be delegated to him.
The minister further recommends that Mr. Marshall be paid a salary at the rate of $6,000 per annum, said salary to be paid from the appropriation provided for the administration of the Agricultural Instruction Act, and that this appointment date from January 15, 1922.

Su-p-ply-Agriculture-Salaries
His appointment was to date a little more than five weeks before he was appointed. He had evidently set to work-if you call it work-five weeks before the government hit upon this scheme. I cannot congratulate the government upon either the ingenuity or the plausibility of the scheme they adopted to turn some of the public funds to Mr. Marshall. Here are funds that parliament voted for the carrying out of the Agricultural Instruction Act. After parliament votes that money for that purpose, and that alone, the government comes along and turns $6,000 a year, as well as expenses, away from the object for which parliament voted the money, and says that it is doing it under the authority of section 38 (c) of the Civil Service Act. That section of the Civil Service Act gives no authority to anybody to do anything-none whatsoever-and does not pretend to. This government had not one atom, not one line, not one letter, not one figment more authority after section 38 (c) was passed than it had before. What did that section say? It reads:
Nothing in this act-
That is the Civil Service Act.
-shall affect-
What?
*-shall aff jet the powers of the Governor in Council with respect to the appointment of any commissioner or other member of any royal or other commission or board, or any deputy head.
Nothing shall affect the powers that now exist to appoint a member of a royal commission. If there had been an act before to enable the government to appoint Duncan Marshall under the Agricultural Instruction vote, to be paid any way in the world, those powers were not affected by tills act, they were neither added to nor subtracted from, but the power never existed before-never did exist. The government had power under the Inquiries Act to appoint somebody for a specific inquiry within the terms of that act, and this section says that wherever the government has had the power before, this act does not take it from them and give it to the Civil Service Commissign. Under this section the government has no added power whatever. It does not purport to give it any added power. The thing is so simple that I really cannot understand the government exercising-I do not know how to describe it-venturing to use this section, or pretending to use this section, to appoint one of their favourites to office. Whatever powers the government had before in respect of the 
appointment of a royal commission or any member of it were not affected by the Civil Service Act amendment of 1921, but if the government did not have the power before it did not get it under this section. Let me put it in another way. If there was doubt in the mind of anyone that the provisions of the Civil Service Act, as they existed, put into the hands of the Civil Service Commission powers that formerly were the government's powers, to appoint a commissioner under the Inquiries Act, or any other act, this section made it clear that there Was no change. The government still has the power and not the Civil Service Commission. But nobody could suggest, to say nothing about arguing, that any appointment could be made under that section. It cannot be made. The government must make its appointment under some other act, and, if at the time that section was passed it had power, under another act, it could use that power and appoint a man. But it did not do that, and why? If it had it under the Inquiries Act, it had it for the purposes of the Inquiries Act, and subject to the restrictions therein embodied. I do not know of any other act under which it could have done it. It could have made an appointment under the Inquiries Act of a royal commission, but it could not do it under this act. I venture to say that, Dnucan Marshall's appointment being based on the provisions of this order in council, he is being paid illegally every dollar he receives, and I say that no matter what the Auditor General has done and without the slightest doubt in my mind. I hope I have made myself clear. If there was power in the government under any act to appoint a commissioner at the time this section was passed, that power the government still has* and the Civil Service Commission did not get that power, but it had to appoint him under the act that existed, and, of course, subject to the provisions of that act. If it had appointed him under the act that existed, he would not be there now. But these hon. gentlemen want to get round that and to make him a salaried officer, so that they affect to do it under the act which gave them no power whatever. That is the extent to which the government has gone to reward a political favourite. I would like the minister, or anybody, to bring down the submission of this order in council, if it ever was submitted, to the Justice department and the ruling of the Justice department upon it. I frequently asked for those things

Supply-Agriculture-Salaries
and never got one yet. I venture to say the hon. gentlemen cannot get a ruling from the Justice department that there is any power whatever in the government, under the Civil Service Act of 1921, to appoint any commissioner at all.

I am glad that we have got to this-I shall not say fight-but to this question. I am not versed in the law, Mr. Chairman, but I assume that when a party is taken into the employ of the government, and paid regularly, it must be in accordance with some law. I know that the Auditor General is there for a purpose. He is not a figure head; I do not know anybody who could put very much past him, and I certainly am not trying to put anything past him, and there has never been a question of doubt as to the legality of Mr. Marshall's appointment. When the advisability of his appointment was first taken up, I did not know what the custom was. This Civil Service Commission was new to me. I was familiar with one commission in the West, and, I might say I believe in the Civil Service Commission. I believe it is necessary to have one, but I knew something of this from hearsay and from reading in the papers, and after I had made inquiries from my deputy and others as to the propriety of calling upon the Civil Service Commission I did so in connection with this, the first appointment I was interested in. I had an interview with them in their board room and I told them something of the situation. I do not know whether hon. members are familiar with all the intricacies of getting an appointment of this nature made. Wc first have to establish the position and then send to the Civil Service Commission for its classification. After they arrive at that stage, they send it back, with the signatures of two members of the commission on it, to the minister who is interested, and it is intimated that if the minister agrees with it, he can sign it. That again goes to the government, and after the government put their O.K. on it, it goes back to the department and then to the Civil Service Commission again in order that they may advertise the position. We discussed every phase of this appointment, and everything was agreed upon with the Civil Service Commission, I may say to my right hon. friend. Even the salary was agreed upon, the amount of salary that such a position was worth and that was necessary to secure an appointee who would be capable of carrying on the work satisfactorily. The question of
salary had to be decided upon in connection with the classification, before advertising could be done. At that time I was not familiar with how long the advertising would take It was arranged with the commission, first that such an appointment was necessary, second that the classification should be worth 86,000 per annum, and that was arranged satisfactorily with the commission. Then I found out that it was going to take an interminable time to get the appointment put through, and also that the advertising would take from two to three, and sometimes four weeks to complete. After the advertising there is the usual rating and examination, and I wanted the appointment filled then, not a* some indefinite date in the future. I had been told by my deputy that he had experienced delays. He has not very much complaint to make against the Civil Service Commission; the only complaint he makes is in connection with the time it takes to make these appointments, and time means everything, especially in connection with farming operations. What farmer would be anxious to buy a seed drill in the middle of harvest or the fall when he wanted it in the spring? That was exactly the position I was in. I did not want this appointment filled after I was dead; I wanted it filled then. I did not want the appointee to go out cutting wood next winter.
The minister does not mean that he wanted the position filled after Mr. Duncan Marshall was dead.

Let my right hon. friend sit down. I may say further that I do not lay any particular blame at the door of the Civil Service Commission. My judgment was borne out in my subsequent experience as to the length of time required, and again I am blaming, not the commission, but the act that determines the actions of the commission and of the rest of us. As the committee is aware, the regulations with respect to hog grading came into force last October. It took ten solid months from the initial step until we got those ten hog graders appointed. The hogs could have been killed, eaten and gone out of sight altogether in those ten months and a new bunch of hogs could have appeared on the scene, been fattened and made ready for the knife while you were getting your graders appointed. I had made an arrangement with Mr. Arkell; I had told him that I would like to see the ten new members of my family. They were assembled at Toronto, and I met them there. This was the first work of this kind ever un-

Supply-Agriculture-Salaries
dertaken on this continent or anywhere else that I knew of, to grade live hogs for the market, and consequently I wanted to see these new appointees. I did not know one of them from Adam; I had never seen them before; I met them in Toronto; I had an hour's talk with them, and I gave them some instructions in regard to their duties. As I say, it took just ten months from the beginning of the operation to get them appointed, and the hogs they graded were not born at the time I started operations. That is what we have to go through in connection with getting appointments made. I do not want to exaggerate this, or I could tell the committee very much worse instances than that, even in my short experience. It is no wonder that anyone who wants to administer a department properly chafes under such conditions. Let me say again that the blame lies, not with the commission, but with the act by which they have to be governed, and these are some of the results. Having regard to that, having regard to the further fact that the necessity for the appointment was agreed upon by the commission and the salary was agreed upon, I say that the only thing left was the time it would take to get the appointment put through. Is there anybody in the country who will say that Mr. Duncan Marshall is not a proper and qualified man for the position? If he cannot, there is no point to all this discussion. If anyone has a recommendation to make on behalf of someone who will better fill the duties that have devolved upon Mr. Marshall, I shall be delighted to have his name and to give his qualifications my best consideration, because I want the very best men obtainable in the Department of Agriculture. Hon. members from Saskatchewan will, I think, admit that when I was administering the department there, I let nothing stand in the way of getting the best obtainable men in my department, and any success obtained there was obtained through that policy. My desire is to pursue the same policy here; but what is the use of making appointments for a particular purpose, if frequently you cannot get them made until the expiry of the time when you really desire them most? Right at this time we want a most important position filled immediately. This will be worth more to us in the next few weeks than if two or three months elapse before the appointment is made. We have, however, to go through the routine; the hands of the Civil Service Commission are tied, and they have to go through it too. That is one of the reasons why this appointment was not made by the Civil Service Commission. Why was it not? The
IMr. Motherwell.]
leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) says that it was made illegally. If it was, I must be a wonderful individual who can jam a political friend through all these devious ways and get him appointed in spite of the law. I would be some mover if I could do that. There is a proviso-my right hon. friend has read it himself-by which a commissioner can be appointed. The conditions stipulated are all justified; they are all true.
Just for fear that this might be overlooked, I may say that a few remarks have been made about the qualifications of Mr. Marshall. If there is in Canada any man better qualified for the work he is doing, I want to find him and I will look upon it as a favour if any person will send in the names of men who are better qualified, either as platform men or as live stock authorities, because we want a man of just such qualifications as those of Mr. Marshall. I have in my hand an Old Country paper, the Live Stock Journal, which discusses the embargo situation. This is not what I say about Mr. Duncan Marshall at all, because I might be prejudiced in his favour. This is a journal that has no object	in being
prejudiced; it is	printed in	the Old
Country, in London, and it is recognized as one of the leading live stock authorities. Under date of May 4-and this was just at the time when there was a good deal of anxiety over there about getting the balance of the embargo off our breeding cattle-this is what it says, at a time by the way when some of the very extreme friends of Mr. Duncan Marshall were trying to make out that he was not exercising his duties properly just at that time. I am not going to read it all unless I am requested to do so, because it is a two-column article. Anyone can call for the paper, and I am not excluding anything derogatory to Mr. Marshall because there is not a line in it of that nature. The article reads in part:
There is a distinct grievance against Canada in seeking to raise this new point of the admission of breeding cattle. It is to be feared that Dr. J. H. Grisdale, the Deputy Minister of Agriculture, and the Hon. Duncan Marshall, Canada's Live Stock Commissioner-
By the way, that is still a new title, which he has not received any more than Commissioner of Agriculture.
-know their business too well for the "amateurs" whom our system of government place at the head of our various departments.
You see, they are playing politics here just as the Opposition do in this House even on a question of agriculture.

Whether I am right or wrong, I understand that this man is not Commissioner of Agriculture, although he has been so styled. Now, I have here the Scottish Farmer, an agricultural journal printed in Glasgow, and this particular copy is of the issue of January 27 of the present year. Referring to a sale of pure-bred cattle which had taken place in Scotland some time previously, the article states:
Lawton's champion Shorton bull was not exported by the man from Stranraer, but by the other Marshall -the Hon. Duncan, the man from the Northwest.
It is well known that four months after parliament prorogued Mr. Marshall and Mr. Dryden were in the Old Country attending auction sales of pure-bred shorthorn cattle; that purchases were made by Mr. Dryden, and that the animals were brought to this country. A question was asked when Mr. Marshall's appointment was under discussion in the House a year ago with regard to his 
action as a breeder of beef cattle. The hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) asked:

The minister stated:
I understand from the newspaper reports that Mr. Marshall has sold out his live stock and has rented his place. He is therefore completely at liberty to represent the government.
Now, he has evidently been very active in attending the auction sales of pure-bred shorthorn cattle in Scotland and elsewhere since he went over to the Old Country. I believe he has made several trips across the Atlantic since the House prorogued in June last and it is rather significant that we have not been able to deal with the matter up to the present time. In view of the statement made by the minister regarding the appointment and the difficulties experienced in connection with the Civil Service Commission, I took occasion some time ago to place some questions on the order paper as to the salary of these two commissioners, who, we were informed, were expected to go to South America to develop a live stock trade between the countries there and Canada. In answer to that question it was stated that Mr. Marshall's salary and expenses to date amounted to $8,952.08, and that Mr. Dryden had received an advance for expenses of $2,000. I would like to know from the minister when Mr. Dryden's services began and when they ended, and whether he was in the employ of the government when he and Mr. Duncan Marshall, according to Mr. Duncan Marshall's own newspaper reports were attending these sales of pure-bred shorthorn cattle in the old land. Mr. Marshall has been a prominent man in this country for a great many years. I remember when he was a candidate for election nearly twenty years ago in an Ontario constituency, on which occa-

Wm. Henderson and Hon. Duncan Marshall dressed in white market coats, beside the steer as he steps off the gang plank on to Scottish soil.
Mr. Duncan Marshall must have got on his feet in order to enable the man with the camera to take a snap, for it is quite apparent he has been through a trying experience because he is bare-headed, while Mr. Henderson is not. Surely this farce has gone far enough, when an active politician can come here, as he did, immediately following the election and make demands upon the government and get those demands granted. He receives a salary of upwards of two thousand dollars more than he could have received had he been appointed by the Civil Service Commission. That is quite a consideration. Now if there is need for economy in this country, and there is every need, if Mr. Marshall can render good and valuable service to this country I have no objection to his doing so but, I do object to him acting in the capacity in which he has been acting since his appointment. He should devote his attention to the work for which he was supposed to be

I do not know
whether these statements of my hon. friend deserve very much attention or not, but inasmuch as they have been made and there has been a good deal of sniping on this question all winter, possibly I had better pay a little attention to them.
Mr. Duncan Marshall when he was over there with Mr. Dryden did not purchase any cattle for himself or anybody else. I cannot imagine the hon. member for Victoria City (Mr. Tolmie) going over to the Old Country and not attending any popular sale, of live stock that was being held. Is that a crime, Mr. Chairman? If it is, I guess Mr. Marshall has committed it. But it is no crime, and it is nonsense to make a complaint about it. As to the letter to the Canadian Countryman, I saw a number of Mr. Marshall's letters, and among others one that he wrote to the Toronto Globe on the question of hog and

bacon grading, and I never saw a better put letter on, that question. He reported just where Canadian bacon fell short of Danish bacon, went into the question in minute detail, and I made the remark at the time having in mind one of my hon. friend's observations, that article alone was worth his entire salary for the year. I believe that still, and if he wrote an account for the British and Canadian journals of the landing of the first cargo of Canadian cattle in Great Britain after they had been debarred for thirty-one years, do you not think that was a very good way to let the people of Canada know just what happened in connection with that notable and historic event? Why, only the other day the whole Agricultural committee of this House, every one of whom had the privilege of inviting two friends, went down to the old historic city of Quebec and saw the first cargo of Canadian cattle shipped from that port via the Canadian National Railway all through. That was an historic event and one that we should commemorate. They did not write it up perhaps as picturesquely as Mr. Marshall might have done, but they gave it due publicity, and I think we should have been derelict in our duty if we had not been there.
My deputy and myself and one or two others went down to Montreal and saw the first cargo of Canadian cattle loaded there for shipment via St. John. Our presence was required there because there was a hitch as to whether they could be shipped via the Canadian Pacific, which went through United States territory part of the way, and we decided that it was not advisable to ship via the Canadian Pacific, which passes through part of Maine. W'e did not want any hitch over some technicality, but apart from that we were desirous of being there to celebrate that notable event. I do not know why we should make one law for ourselves and another for Mr. Duncan Marshall. We do not want him to hide his light under a bushel.
No danger.

I am sure my hon. friend has read Mr. Marshall's articles with a great deal of pleasure. Mr. Marshall, it appears, has committed the heinous offence of being defeated twice in politics. Well, Mr. Chairman, if that were a hanging matter a lot of us would be missing here, and if my hon. friend from South Oxford lives long enough it may be he will suffer a defeat himself, and then he will be a little more charitable to those of us who have experienced it not once but several times. That is what we call small potatoes and mighty few in a hill-to make a statement of that kind about a man who had

As to Mr. Marshall being down in Florida, I thought I dealt with that last winter. That was an exhibition where the Department of the Interior had an exhibit, and that exhibit was run all through the Conservative regime, and I think through the preceding Liberal regime. The leader of the Opposition was very hilarious over the exhibition in Florida [DOT] to which we sent an exhibit. I do not think he knew that that same exhibit was being run there while he was Prime Minister of this country. At an exhibition of that kind where you get a large concourse of people in great big auditoriums, it is an advantage to a country to have a man with Mr. Marshall's capacity for filling a building and occupying a platform acceptably. I have been at some of these gatherings with him, and I do not know anybody who can better captivate an American audience than he can. I attended the International Dry Farming Conference at Colorado Springs and Billings with Mr. Marshall, and I can tell my hon. friends that he was the lion of the day with the guests; there is no question about that, and what is more, we have direct information that a number of immigrants came to Canada as a result of Mr. Marshall's address at that meeting in Florida. I saw in the Department of the Interior whole sheets of clippings from American papers reporting that meeting, and if we had had to pay for that advertising space in cash it would have cost us $10,000. That was the speech he made at a place where we have been holding exhibits for ten or twelve years, and yet all kinds of ridicule were heaped upon Mr. Marshall for this globe trotting as if it was the first time we ever had an exhibition in Florida. I do not think the leader of the Opposition knew anything about where our exhibitions were being held. He never dreamed of one being held in Florida or he would never have made the foolish remarks he did with respect to Mr. Marshall's speech there.
The hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) says he does not know anything about Mr. Marshall's qualifications. Well, should not that be the chief consideration? Should it have been my first duty to have inquired how many times he was defeated at the elections before I opened negotiations with him, or should I have suggested, as is done in some cases "If you will apply to the
Civil Service Commission you will at least have a chance of getting through?" Should I have sent in a blank form to be filled in and returned to Mr. Foran, the Secretary of the Civil Service Commission, or should I have inquired into Mr. Marshall's qualifications to fill the post? I think that his qualifications were the first consideration, and no one has yet challenged his fitness to do the work that has been allotted to him since his appointment-not one challenge has been made. Therefore I think this talk on the part of my hon. friends, while it may be quite justifiable from their standpoint, is done for the purpose of raising a little hurrah so that they may get it featured in a spectacular way in the press in the hope of making the public believe that there is something doing on their part by reason of their stand on this question. That is all this talk is for; there is no challenge as to Mr. Marshall's fitness. It seems to me that if we placed a gentleman at this work who did not know the A.B.C. about politics and was otherwise disqualified the mere fact that he was never in politics would certainly not overshadow his ineligibility. I say again, the first essential consideration is service on the part of Mr. Marshall for the money he gets. I submit that Mr. Marshall is earning his salary as fully and efficiently as any hon. member in this House or any other official in the public service.

If I were in the position of Minister of Agriculture I think I should be inclined to take the same attitude. It is better not to see the point; that is convenient for the minister. The leader of the Opposition has made a charge that the appointment of Mr. Duncan Marshall to this1 unmentionable position-no one seems to be able to name it-was illegal, and that the salary he has been receiving ever since has been illegally given. Not only has the leader of the Opposition made that charge but, I think, he has very successfully proven his case. The only answer the Minister of Agriculture has been able to make to that point was the reading of an article from swine English paper. Personally I fail to see the connection between the editorial he read and the charge made by the leader of the Opposition. It is said in this editorial, among other things, that Mr. Marshall was a live stock commissioner. The 'minister himself denied that. That means that the article was wrong in the first place with regard to the position and suggested, to me at least, that it may have

But that is not a recommendation for Mr. Marshall. I wish now to enter a brief and emphatic protest against this appointment. I should have done this last year, but I refrained for two reasons. In the first place we were given the assurance that the appointment of Mr. Marshall was temporary, that it would not last more than six months. I, of course* took that assurance seriously; I thought it was true. A year later I find it is not. In the second place I did not protest last year because I happened to be the opponent of Mr. Marshall in the last election, and I know it is difficult for some people to disassociate any attack that I might make in regard to his appointment from political propaganda. That we do not know; we have to wait until the minister tries to find out just exactly how much Mr. Marshall has cost the country. But he was appointed at this salary and was 
given this office shortly after the last election.

Mr. Marshall at that time was appointed Commissioner of Agriculture. That position was considered by the former government as being unnecessary-at least, I unden

That is unfortunately true in this particular regard, but if the minister i->
very anxious to get the evidence and will give me ten days' time, I think I can procure at least enough evidence to justify the statement which I have just made.
The main point I want to make is that this country cannot afford to have two Ministers of Agriculture. If it takes two Liberal statesmen to make one minister then I suggest that they get one salary between them. 1 think that is a fair proposition.
