There is, in my opinion, a serious aspect to this question, which the Minister of Agiiculture (Mr. Motherwell) seems to misapprehend or, for his own purposes, seeks to evade. The case as presented by the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) is, to my mind, a serious case and one in respect to which the committee is entitled to some explanation from the government. If the Minister of Agriculture does not see fit to give the explanation or is unable to give it, then I must appeal to the law officers of the Crown or the Minister of Justice (Sir Lomer Gouin), sitting in this House at this time, to explain to the committee how it comes about that a man is appointed to the service of the Crown upon what appears, on an examination of the statutes, to be in direct opposition to the letter and spirit of the law, why also that man for the past sixteen or seventeen months has been drawing his salary through the ordinary channels through which salaries are paid, and I presume that the cheques representing that salary have likewise passed through the Auditor General's office. If the statement of the law and the facts are as my right hon. friend has stated them, the committee is entitled to a very clear and definite statement by the government how this matter came about. We find an order in council passed on the 7th February, 1922. The new government, the present government, took office, if I remember rightly, on the last day of the preceding year, so that about five weeks had elapsed before the order in council in question was passed. The order provides for the appointment of a commissioner in these terms:
It is considered advisable that a commissioner be appointed under section 38C of the Civil Service Act as amended by chapter 22 of the statutes of 1921, to conduct the investigation indicated above and to inquire into such other agricultural problems as may [DOT] be desirable and necessary.
Then the order enacts:
That Mr. Duncan Marshall of Olds, Alberta, be appointed as a commissioner for the above purpose. . . [Mr. Irvine. 1
and further that Mr, Marshall be paid a salary at the rate of $6,000 per annum, said salary to be paid from the appropriation provided for the administration of the Agricultural Instruction Act and that this appoint-men date from the 15th January, 1922.
The appointment has been made under a statute definitely and clearly stated in the order. It is section 38C of the act of 1921 amending the Civil Service Act. First let me point out to the committee that under the Civil Service Act there is no power to appoint a commissioner. That is clear and definite. Is there under the amendment? This is the amendment cited, section 38C:
Nothing in this act shall affect the powers of the Governor in Council with respect to the appointment of any commissioner or other member of any royal or other commission or board, or any deputy head.
Meaning in plain, clear language that any power which existed in the Governor in Council to appoint commissioners should be retained by the Governor in Council notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act. The language is clear and express. What power is there in the Governor in Council to appoint a commissioner? What power ever was there? There is no such power under the Civil Service Act. There was power under the Inquiries Act and it is the only power whereby a commissioner can be appointed or a royal commission can be issued. If a commissioner is appointed under that act, that act prescribes the procedure, limits the authority, directs how the investigation shall be conducted. But he is not appointed under that act at all; he is appointed expressly under section 38C of an amendment to the Civil Service Act which confers no right upon the government nor the Governor in Council to appoint a commissioner for any purpose whatever. Mark this also, Mr. Chairman. If the commissioner is appointed under the Inquiries Act, he is paid under that act and according to the terms of that act; but under the order in council in question it is said that he is appointed under section 38C which I have read, and he is to be paid, in violation of the vote of this parliament, from money appropriated for investigations in regard to agriculture. This parliament expressly voted a certain sum of money, $1,100,000, for a specific purpose. The appointment and payment of a commissioner was not one of those purposes, and there is no power under this order in council legally to pay Mr. Duncan Marshall one dollar of salary. How the matter has slipped through the Auditor General's office, I cannot imagine. How it has slipped through the Justice department, I cannot imagine. I appeal to the Miriister of Justice to make

That charge has not been answered; that - charge has been absolutely avoided by the Minister of Agriculture. We have had no word from the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), whose name is brought into prominence in connection with this matter. These are the two objections we take, and take most pointedly. We want to know why the appointment was made, what justification there was for it in law, and why the Auditor General allowed those cheques to be paid if he allowed that.

How could the word "affect" be used if there is a power given?
Nothing in this act shall affect the powers of the Governor in Council with respect to the appointment of any commissioner.
Assuming that there were powers, which there were, this act does not affect those powers. Consequently the Governor in Council is thrown back upon the powers that there were. He is not given any more powers and he must exercise the powers that there were because no further powers are given. If the minister would just reserve this and take a little time to think it out there is no question but that the matter is not even debatable because no powers are given at all. The Governor in Council has to take all the powers there were, and those powers are reserved to the Governor in Council. The act makes quite clear that they are not affected and not transferred to the commission. What powers were there before? There were powers under the Inquiries Act. The government might have exercised those powers, but in the exercise of them they could not have made this appointment. They could not under the Inquiries Act have appointed a commissioner and paid him out of the Agricultural Instruction vote. They had to pay him out of
the vote applicable to the purpose. That is where there is a misappropriation of funds. The miscellaneous vote of parliament is applicable for a purpose. They did not want to go to that vote. Perhaps there were no moneys there. The only way they could appoint a commissioner was under the Inquiries Act, under the powers given them prior to the passing of section 38 C of the Civil Service Act. Further, had they appointed under the Inquiries Act, the inquirer would have had the powers given by that act and no other. All the restraints and restrictions of that act would have applied. That is the only kind of a commissioner they could have appointed. The powers to appoint that commissioner were reserved by section 38 C, but no new powers were given. If the minister had had time to go into it, and had given full consideration to the actual meaning of the English words,
I think he never would have expressed his opinion as a lawyer that they had the power. I suggest that he consult the officers of the department and bring an official opinion to this House. I confidently say that he cannot set them to give an opinion that any powers whatever are given to the government by section 38 C of the act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. member
did not ask me to give him the opinion of the officers of my department. He asked me for my opinion and I gave him an answer, taking section 38 C, the Inquiries Act and the order in council in conjunction-I gave my opinion candidly.
That what?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That we had the
right to make that appointment, and the payments we made.

I think the minister means that his opinion is that a commissioner could be appointed under the Inquiries Act for the purpose of carrying out the object of that act, buit he will not find'-any one of those objects have any connection! with this man's work. He will find he has note called one witness and he will find that he has made absolutely no report, as called for by that section.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That is another
question, but if you read section 2 of chapter 104 of the revised statutes, you will find that the Governor in Council may, whenever he deems it expedient, cause inquiry to be made into and concerning any matter connected with the good government of Canada or the conduct of any part of the public business thereof. I do not know what Mr. Marshall has done or
Supply-Agriculture-Salaries

omitted to do, but as to the legal point which has been raised, I consider that the appointment was' regular and that the payment was also regular.
But I think the minister is referring to just exactly what he read, namely the kind of inquiry called for under the Inquiries Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

I agree with
that; there is no question about it, but this is not under this act. There was the power under that to have the inquiry as called for by the act, and that has not been done and is not being done. It was never thought of. The job was, thought of and the job is still going on. The minister has not answered what, to my mind, is the most vital thing. Here we have an order in council which, I agree with him, can only be supported under chapter 104. What right or what power is there in the case of a commissioner appointed under that section, to charge the expenses and cost to this agricultural vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Because it was an
investigation in regard to agricultural matters.

It may possibly be, although I do not think so, that under the Audit Act, which has to do with our appropriations, we could charge to' a specific vote the cost of an inquiry which had to do absolutely with that one particular vote. But that is not the case here at all. We have here a concrete vote of $1,100,000 in connection with the Agricultural Instruction Act. It is not pretended that Mr. Duncan Marshall was engaged in England in connection with that matter. It is not pretended that he went down to Florida in connection with that. It is not pretended by the minister in charge of this department that there is a word of truth in the suggestion that he was acting as a commissioner to find out something in connection with the Agricultural Instruction Act. He went to Florida for the purpose of getting immigrants to come to Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is a matter of fact. I was not questioned on the facts. It was on a point of law and it is on that question that I have given my opinion.
Perhaps I should not press my hon. friend any further on the point.

Before the vote is taken, may I point out that the salary of Mr. Mar-

shall is not taken out of this item, but out of another item?
It has just as much right to be taken out of this as out of the other one.
It has not.
The matter as to where the government may choose an item to misappropriate money is not a matter of concern to this House. The government has no right to take it out of either vote-none whatever.

There are two items; one is for a grant to the provinces of Canada for the purpose of assisting and encouraging agricultural instruction, grants to be made on a proportionate basis. That is item No. 51.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Item 14 on page 8 of the estimates is the one under consideration.
Amendment (Mr. Irvine) negatived: Yeas 39; nays 82.
If the minister is confident of his opinion, will he undertake to grant a fiat that this matter may be tested?
Oh, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: A fiat for what?
A fiat to test the validity of the payment to Duncan Marshall under this appointment by order in council.
That is childish. Take your medicine.
We will get the medicine first, and then we shall see who takes it. Will the minister undertake so to do?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I will not undertake that to-night. If I have a petition to that effect, I will consider it.
The minister should have considered the matter before he gave his opinion to-night.

Item agreed to.
Progress reported.
